courses.title: Bridge Watchkeeping
courses.description: Eight stages covering COLREGs, recognition, collision avoidance, buoyage, traffic separation and AIS.

lessons.title: How Helmlore teaches
lessons.intro: Different parts of Helmlore have different purposes.
facts: Learn
Teaching screens explain the subject before you are tested.
Practise
Guided simulators let you apply it with coaching.
Assess
Knowledge checks and mock exams test material after it has been taught. A wrong answer is feedback, not the end of the course.

lessons.title: Your own vessel
lessons.intro: Before interpreting other traffic, know the vessel from which you are observing it.
facts: Own vessel
The vessel you are controlling is your own vessel. In Helmlore it uses the personal vessel profile, or Watch One as the default.
Bow & stern
Bow means the front of the vessel. Stern means the rear.
Port & starboard
Facing forward, port is your left side and starboard is your right side. These terms stay with the vessel, not the edge of the screen.

lessons.title: Direction around you
lessons.intro: Traffic is described relative to your vessel as well as by compass bearing.
facts: Ahead / astern
Ahead is in front of the bow. Astern is behind the stern.
Beam
The beam direction is approximately 90° to either side of the vessel.
Quarter
The quarters are the rear-side sectors between the beam and stern.

lessons.title: Heading
lessons.intro: Heading tells you the direction the vessel’s bow is pointing.
facts: Heading
A heading of 090° means the bow is pointing east.
It can change
Turning the vessel changes heading.
Not always your track
Wind, tide and current can mean the direction you move over the ground is different from heading.

lessons.title: COG & SOG
lessons.sub: How you move over the ground
lessons.intro: Electronic navigation commonly shows Course Over Ground and Speed Over Ground.
facts: COG
Course Over Ground is the direction your vessel is actually moving across the Earth.
SOG
Speed Over Ground is how fast the vessel is moving over the Earth.
Compare with heading
Heading and COG can differ. That difference is useful information, not automatically an instrument error.

lessons.title: Lookout first
lessons.intro: No screen replaces the basic duty to maintain a proper lookout.
facts: Sight and hearing
Look outside and listen.
All available means
Use radar, AIS and other appropriate aids when available, but as supporting information.
Build the picture
Keep updating what vessels are doing; do not make one observation and stop watching.

lessons.title: How Helmlore reads lights & shapes
lessons.sub: Four visual ideas — four matching explanations
lessons.intro: Start with four things you can actually see in the approved visual cards. Extra marine words are explained later, at the point where you first need them.
facts: Masthead light
White. A forward-facing navigation light fitted on the vessel’s centreline.
Sidelights
Red is port and green is starboard. Which one or ones you can see depends on your viewing aspect.
Ball
A black round day shape. It is used alone or in prescribed combinations to show particular vessel conditions.
Cone — apex down
A black cone with the pointed end facing downward. “Apex” simply means the pointed tip of the cone.

lessons.title: Ordinary power-driven vessel lights
lessons.sub: First recognise the basic navigation lights
lessons.intro: Start with an ordinary power-driven vessel underway. Where you are looking from — the viewing aspect — changes which lights are visible.
facts: Masthead light
A white light on the vessel’s centreline. It shines from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam on either side. “Abaft” means behind; the beam is the vessel’s widest point across the middle.
Port sidelight
Red. It is fitted on the vessel’s port, or left, side when looking forward from onboard.
Starboard sidelight
Green. It is fitted on the vessel’s starboard, or right, side when looking forward from onboard.
Sternlight
White and directed around the after part of the vessel. From directly astern this is the key ordinary navigation light.
Why the picture changes
A light can be fitted to the vessel but invisible to you because you are outside that light’s viewing sector.

lessons.title: Viewing aspect changes the picture
lessons.sub: Ahead, port side, starboard side and astern
lessons.intro: Aspect means where YOU are looking at the other vessel from. The same vessel can therefore present a different light picture without changing what it is doing.
facts: Ahead
Looking toward the bow. Both red and green sidelights can be visible together with the applicable masthead light or lights.
Port-side aspect
You are looking at the vessel’s port side, so the red sidelight can be visible together with the applicable white light or lights.
Starboard-side aspect
You are looking at the vessel’s starboard side, so the green sidelight can be visible together with the applicable white light or lights.
Astern
You are looking toward the vessel’s stern. The white sternlight is the key ordinary navigation light directed toward you.

lessons.title: Day shapes — learn the silhouettes
lessons.intro: Day shapes are black shapes shown in daylight. Learn the silhouette, number, order and orientation. “Apex” simply means the pointed end of a cone.
facts: Ball
A black round shape. One ball is the basic anchor day shape. Other vessel conditions use balls in combinations.
Cone — apex up
A black cone with its pointed tip UP. The direction of the point matters.
Cone — apex down
A black cone with its pointed tip DOWN. A sailing vessel also being propelled by machinery uses this day shape.
Diamond
A black diamond shape. It appears in several prescribed combinations, including some towing and restricted-manoeuvrability displays.
Cylinder
A tall black rectangular-looking shape. A vessel constrained by her draught may exhibit a cylinder.

lessons.title: Special vessel-status patterns
lessons.sub: Learn what the activity means as well as the colours
lessons.intro: These all-round light patterns tell you about a vessel’s condition or work. Learn the plain-English meaning first, then the recognition pattern.
facts: Not under command — red over red
The vessel cannot manoeuvre as required by the Rules because of an exceptional circumstance and therefore cannot keep out of another vessel’s way.
Restricted in ability to manoeuvre — red • white • red
The nature of the vessel’s work restricts her ability to manoeuvre as required by the Rules.
Trawling — green over white
Trawling is fishing by dragging a trawl net or other fishing apparatus through the water.
Fishing other than trawling — red over white
Fishing with gear that restricts manoeuvrability, but not by trawling. This COLREG status does not mean every boat simply using a fishing rod.

lessons.title: Anchor, aground, towing, pilot, dredging & mine clearance
lessons.sub: Six different displays — six different meanings
lessons.intro: Finish the teaching section with six separate vessel situations. Match each picture to its explanation before moving to the final check.
facts: At anchor
A vessel secured by her anchor rather than underway. The basic day shape is one black ball; prescribed anchor lights depend on vessel length.
Aground
A vessel whose hull is touching the ground. It adds the prescribed aground signals to the anchor display; by day the familiar signal is three black balls vertically.
Towing astern
A vessel towing another vessel or object behind her. Towing has additional prescribed masthead/towing lights, and long tows require a diamond by day.
Pilot vessel
A vessel engaged on pilotage duty. Its distinctive night identification is white over red; when underway, the required ordinary navigation lights are also shown.
Dredging / underwater operations
A restricted-in-ability-to-manoeuvre operation. Two red lights or balls mark the obstructed side; two green lights or diamonds mark the side on which another vessel may pass.
Mine clearance
A vessel engaged in mine-clearance operations shows three additional all-round green lights at night or three balls by day. The special display warns other vessels to keep well clear.

lessons.title: The language of sound
lessons.intro: First learn the building blocks and which appliances vessels carry.
facts: Short blast
About one second.
Prolonged blast
Four to six seconds. Helmlore uses 4.5 seconds for training playback.
12 m or more
A whistle is required.
20 m or more
A bell is required in addition to a whistle.
100 m or more
A gong is required in addition to whistle and bell.
Under 12 m
If the prescribed appliances are not carried, some other means of making an efficient sound signal is required.

lessons.title: Vessel status — plain English
lessons.intro: Before learning the fog signal, learn the vessel-status words. The abbreviations describe why a vessel may have limits on how she can manoeuvre.
facts: NUC — Not Under Command

Something exceptional means the vessel cannot manoeuvre as the COLREGs require and therefore cannot keep out of another vessel’s way. Think: an abnormal problem has taken away normal manoeuvring ability.
RAM — Restricted in Ability to Manoeuvre

The nature of the vessel’s work restricts her ability to manoeuvre as the COLREGs require. Examples include dredging, surveying, underwater work, cable or pipeline work, replenishment underway and some towing operations. Think: the job she is doing limits her.
CBD — Constrained by Draught

A power-driven vessel whose draught, compared with the available depth of water, severely restricts her ability to deviate from the course she is following. Think: deep vessel + limited depth = very little room to move sideways.
Sailing vessel
Under the COLREG definition, a vessel under sail counts as a sailing vessel only when any fitted propelling machinery is not being used.
Engaged in fishing
This means fishing with gear such as nets, lines or trawls that restrict manoeuvrability. Ordinary trolling or gear that does not restrict manoeuvrability does not qualify.
Why this matters in fog

NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing, fishing, and a vessel towing or pushing use the Rule 35(c) restricted-visibility signal: one prolonged followed by two short, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes. The sound does not tell you which one of those statuses it is — it tells you to consider that the other vessel may have particular limitations.

lessons.title: Manoeuvring in sight
lessons.intro: These signals state what a power-driven vessel is doing when vessels are in sight of one another.
facts: • One short
I am altering my course to starboard.
•• Two short
I am altering my course to port.
••• Three short
I am operating astern propulsion.
Important
Three short does not mean simply “I am going backwards”; it states that astern propulsion is being operated.

lessons.title: Overtaking, doubt & bends
lessons.intro: Narrow-channel overtaking and warning signals have distinctive patterns.
facts: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side.
I intend to overtake you on your port side.
Agreement by the vessel being overtaken.
At least five short and rapid blasts: doubt about the other vessel’s intentions/actions or doubt whether sufficient action is being taken.
One prolonged when nearing an obscured bend/area of a channel or fairway; an approaching vessel within hearing answers with one prolonged.

lessons.title: Fog — vessels underway
lessons.intro: In or near restricted visibility, signals identify status and activity. They apply by day or night.
facts: Power-driven making way
One prolonged, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
Power-driven stopped, no way
Two prolonged, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
NUC / RAM / CBD / sailing / fishing
One prolonged followed by two short, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes. These terms are introduced in the plain-English vessel-status lesson.
Towing or pushing
One prolonged followed by two short.
Last vessel of a manned tow
One prolonged followed by three short, when practicable immediately after the towing vessel.
Rigid composite unit
Treated as a power-driven vessel.

lessons.title: Fog — anchor, aground & pilot
lessons.intro: Bell and gong patterns matter just as much as whistle patterns.
facts: Anchor under 100 m
Rapid bell for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute.
Anchor 100 m or more
Rapid bell forward, then rapid gong aft, each about 5 seconds.
Aground
Anchor bell signal plus three distinct bell strokes immediately before and after the rapid ringing.
Fishing / RAM at anchor
When carrying out their work at anchor, use the Rule 35(c) whistle signal instead of the ordinary anchor signal.
Pilot vessel
When engaged on pilotage duty may add four short blasts to the appropriate Rule 35 signal.
Attention, distress & watchkeeping
Know the difference between attracting attention, indicating distress, and making an ordinary COLREG sound signal.
Rule 36
A vessel may make light or sound signals to attract attention provided they cannot be mistaken for an authorised signal, and may direct a searchlight without embarrassing another vessel.
Rule 37
A vessel in distress and requiring assistance uses or exhibits the signals described in Annex IV.
Examples
SOS, MAYDAY, red flares/rockets, orange smoke and continuous sounding of fog-signalling apparatus are among recognised distress indications.
Restricted visibility
Hearing is part of the lookout. Rule 35 signals are required in or near restricted visibility, not only in fog.
Bridge habit
Hear the pattern, identify only what it actually tells you, then maintain lookout and apply the relevant steering and sailing rules.

lessons.title: Meet your bridge display
lessons.sub: Own vessel, target, range and bearing
lessons.scenario: cross_stbd
lessons.summary: Learn what you are looking at before you touch any controls.
points: Own vessel
The white vessel symbol represents you. It starts in the centre of the simulator display.
Target
The red vessel symbol is the other vessel — the target.
Range
Distance to the target is shown in nautical miles.
Target sector
A plain-language position such as starboard bow or port bow.
steps: radarDisplay
At the start of every tutorial scenario, the white vessel in the centre of the display is your own vessel. The red vessel is the target.
og
The white vessel starting in the centre is always your own vessel. In the power-driven lessons, that vessel represents the selected training vessel.
tg
The red vessel is the target vessel. At the start, it is positioned around your own vessel according to the encounter being taught.
rangeMetric
Range is the distance between you and the target. NM means nautical miles.
sectorMetric
Target sector tells you where the vessel is relative to your bow: ahead, port, starboard, beam, quarter or astern.

lessons.title: CPA & TCPA
lessons.scenario: cross_stbd
lessons.summary: Learn the two numbers used constantly when assessing another vessel.
points: CPA
Closest Point of Approach: predicted minimum passing distance if courses and speeds remain unchanged.
TCPA
Time to CPA: how long until that closest point occurs.
Trend
A low CPA with positive TCPA deserves attention.
Reassess
CPA/TCPA change when either vessel manoeuvres.
steps: cpaMetric
CPA means Closest Point of Approach. It predicts the minimum passing distance if both vessels maintain their present courses and speeds.
tcpaMetric
TCPA means Time to Closest Point of Approach. A positive value means that predicted closest point is still ahead in time.
radarDisplay
Never use one number in isolation. Keep watching the target, the trend, the bearing and the developing situation.

lessons.title: Port & starboard
lessons.sub: Know which side the target is on
lessons.scenario: cross_stbd
lessons.summary: Build the basic language used throughout COLREG collision avoidance.
points: Port
Left side of the vessel when facing forward.
Starboard
Right side of the vessel when facing forward.
Bow
Front of the vessel.
Quarter
Rear side area, between beam and stern.
steps: sectorMetric
This encounter starts with the target on your STARBOARD side — the right-hand side of your own vessel when you are facing forward.
radarDisplay
Port and starboard are always relative to your own vessel and its heading, not simply the left or right edge of the tablet.

lessons.title: Using the helm
lessons.sub: Order rudder and read the response
lessons.scenario: cross_stbd
lessons.summary: Learn the difference between ordered rudder, actual rudder and rate of turn.
points: Ordered rudder
What you ask the steering system to do.
Actual rudder
What the rudder has physically reached.
Rate of turn
How quickly the vessel heading is changing.
Midships
Returns the ordered rudder to zero.
steps: helmControlPanel
This is the helm control. Drag or tap the scale, use the 5° buttons, or press MIDSHIPS.
rudderInstrument
The instrument above shows the ACTUAL rudder angle. It moves progressively toward your ordered rudder.
helmControlPanel
Try ordering STARBOARD 5°. Then press MIDSHIPS. Watch the actual rudder follow the command.

lessons.title: Crossing situation
lessons.scenario: cross_stbd
lessons.summary: Recognise a power-driven crossing encounter and understand give-way / stand-on roles.
points: Rule 15
When two power-driven vessels are crossing so as to involve risk of collision, the vessel which has the other on her starboard side shall keep out of the way.
Rule 16
The give-way vessel should take early and substantial action to keep well clear.
Rule 17
The stand-on vessel initially keeps course and speed, while continuing to monitor.
Avoid ahead
Where circumstances admit, the give-way vessel should avoid crossing ahead.
steps: sectorMetric

In this lesson, two power-driven vessels are in sight of one another, crossing so as to involve risk of collision. The target is on your starboard side, so your own vessel is the give-way vessel under Rule 15.
cpaMetric
Use CPA and TCPA as part of the assessment, but keep a proper lookout and use all available means to judge risk of collision.
helmControlPanel
Under Rules 15 and 16, the give-way vessel must keep out of the way and take early and substantial action. Where circumstances admit, avoid crossing ahead of the vessel on your starboard side.

lessons.title: Head-on situation
lessons.scenario: head_on
lessons.summary: Recognise reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses.
points: Recognise
Two power-driven vessels meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses.
Action
Each power-driven vessel shall alter course to starboard.
Passing
Each vessel passes on the port side of the other.
Monitor
Continue checking the other vessel is also acting.
steps: radarDisplay
Two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses so as to involve risk of collision. The target is essentially ahead.
helmControlPanel
Under Rule 14, each vessel shall alter course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other.

lessons.title: Overtaking
lessons.scenario: overtake
lessons.summary: Learn why the overtaking vessel carries the responsibility.
points: Overtaking vessel
A vessel coming up from more than 22.5° abaft the beam is overtaking.
Give-way
The overtaking vessel keeps out of the way.
Until clear
Responsibility continues until finally past and clear.
Doubt
If in doubt whether you are overtaking, assume that you are.
steps: radarDisplay
In this scenario, your own vessel is coming up from astern of the target in the Rule 13 overtaking sector — more than 22.5 degrees abaft the target vessel’s beam.
sectorMetric
Under Rule 13, the overtaking vessel shall keep out of the way. A later change of bearing does not turn it into a crossing situation or remove that duty until finally past and clear.

lessons.title: Power meets sail
lessons.scenario: power_vs_sail
lessons.summary: Understand the normal power-versus-sail relationship — and that other rules can override it.
points: Rule 18
Except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require, a power-driven vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a sailing vessel.
Not absolute
Overtaking, narrow channels, TSS and special vessel status can change the analysis.
Sailing means sailing
If propulsion machinery is being used, the vessel is treated as power-driven.
Look first
Always identify the actual situation before applying a simple hierarchy.
steps: radarDisplay
The target in this training encounter is a sailing vessel under sail, with propelling machinery not being used.
sectorMetric

Under Rule 18, except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require, a power-driven vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a sailing vessel. Always identify the actual situation before applying that hierarchy.

lessons.title: Your first coached watch
lessons.scenario: cross_stbd
lessons.summary: Run a complete collision encounter with beginner coaching and spoken warnings.
points: Observe
Identify target side, range, CPA and TCPA.
Decide
Work out whether you are give-way or stand-on.
Act
Make any avoiding action early and obvious enough to be understood.
Check
Keep monitoring until the vessels are past and clear.
steps: radarDisplay

This is your first complete coached watch. At the start, the white vessel in the centre is your own vessel and the red vessel is the target. Begin by identifying the target’s position and whether risk of collision is developing.
sectorMetric
In this constructed power-driven crossing exercise, the target begins on your starboard side, so your own vessel is the give-way vessel under Rule 15.
helmControlPanel
Use the helm and, if useful, engine controls. Watch how your decisions change CPA and the target geometry.
alert
Guided mode gives visual and spoken warnings as the situation becomes close. Continue monitoring until the exercise ends.

lessons.title: Lookout, safe speed & collision risk
lessons.intro: Before deciding who gives way, establish the traffic picture and decide whether risk of collision exists.
facts: Proper lookout
Maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing as well as by all available means appropriate to the circumstances.
Safe speed
Proceed at a safe speed so effective avoiding action can be taken and the vessel can be stopped within an appropriate distance.
Risk of collision
Use all available means appropriate to determine whether risk exists. If in doubt, risk is deemed to exist.
Compass bearing
An appreciably steady bearing of an approaching vessel can indicate collision risk; risk can still exist with bearing change, especially with a large vessel, tow or close range.

lessons.title: Early, positive avoiding action
lessons.intro: Correct classification is only useful if the action that follows is clear, early and effective.
facts: Positive and in ample time
Avoiding action should be positive, made in ample time and with due regard to good seamanship.
Make it obvious
Course and/or speed changes should, if circumstances admit, be large enough to be readily apparent; avoid a succession of small alterations.
Safe passing distance
The action must result in passing at a safe distance.
Check the result
Keep checking the effectiveness of the action until the other vessel is finally past and clear.
Slow or stop
If necessary, slacken speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing propulsion.

lessons.title: Overtaking & head-on
lessons.intro: These two encounter families have strong rules that remain easy to apply when recognised early.
facts: Overtaking sector
More than 22.5° abaft the beam. If in doubt, assume overtaking.
Overtaking duty continues
The overtaking vessel keeps out of the way until finally past and clear.
Head-on
Power-driven vessels meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses with risk of collision each alter to starboard.
Head-on doubt
If in doubt whether a head-on situation exists, assume it does and act accordingly.

lessons.title: Crossing & stand-on escalation
lessons.intro: Learn both sides of the crossing rule — including what happens when the expected give-way action does not happen.
facts: Target on your starboard
You are the give-way vessel. Keep out of the way and, if circumstances admit, avoid crossing ahead.
Target on your port
You are normally stand-on: keep course and speed initially.
Rule 17(a)(ii)
The stand-on vessel may take action when it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.
Rule 17(b)
When collision cannot be avoided by give-way action alone, the stand-on vessel shall take such action as will best aid avoidance.
Power crossing caution
A power-driven stand-on vessel acting under 17(a)(ii) should, if circumstances admit, not alter to port for a vessel on her own port side.

lessons.title: Sailing vessels & responsibilities
lessons.intro: Stage 5 explicitly includes sailing-vessel encounters so the learner does not apply power-v-power crossing logic to every target.
facts: Opposite tacks
Port tack gives way to starboard tack.
Same tack
The windward sailing vessel gives way to the leeward vessel.
Uncertain tack
A port-side-wind vessel that cannot determine whether the other sailing vessel has wind on port or starboard keeps out of the way.
Power vs sail
A power-driven vessel underway normally keeps out of the way of a sailing vessel when Rule 18 applies.
Motor-sailing
If machinery is propelling the vessel, treat it as power-driven for collision responsibilities.
Overtaking still wins
Rule 13 applies notwithstanding the other in-sight rules: an overtaking vessel keeps out of the way.

lessons.title: Hierarchy, special waters & restricted visibility
lessons.intro: The final lesson prevents the common mistake of treating every encounter as a simple crossing problem.
facts: Rule 18 responsibilities
Power-driven vessels underway keep out of the way of NUC, RAM, fishing and sailing vessels as specified by Rule 18, subject to Rules 9, 10 and 13.
Narrow channels
Rule 9 adds duties including keeping near the starboard outer limit where safe and practicable and not impeding certain vessels.
Traffic separation
Rule 10 governs conduct in TSS but does not remove the other collision-avoidance duties.
Restricted visibility
When vessels are not in sight in or near restricted visibility, use Rule 19 rather than normal Rules 11–18 encounter labels.
Rule 19 caution
For a vessel detected by radar alone, avoid an alteration to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than one being overtaken, so far as possible.

lessons.title: What AIS actually is
lessons.body: AIS automatically exchanges identity and movement information between suitably equipped vessels and shore stations. Its great strength is situational awareness: it can help you identify a contact and understand the electronic traffic picture.
pts: Identity, target tracking and extra situational information.
That every vessel is transmitting AIS or that every transmitted field is correct.
Correlate the AIS target with what you can see and, where fitted, radar.
AIS does not create a new right-of-way system.
lessons.call: AIS is an additional source of navigational information. It supports the watch; it does not replace the watch.

lessons.title: Read the target — but question the data
lessons.body: Separate what the target reports into useful groups. Identity and vessel particulars help tell you who or what the contact may be. Dynamic information describes present movement. Some voyage information is manually entered and can be old or simply wrong.
pts: Name, MMSI, call sign and ship type can help identify a target.
Position, COG and SOG update automatically from connected sensors.
Destination, draught, ETA and navigational status may depend on human input.
A fresh-looking screen can still contain stale or erroneous source data.
lessons.call: Treat AIS data as information to verify, not truth to obey. A convincing ship name does not make the rest of the transmitted data accurate.

lessons.title: COG is not heading
lessons.body: Course over ground is the direction the vessel is actually moving across the earth. Heading is where its bow points. Current, tide and leeway can make the two values different, so they answer different questions.
pts: Direction of movement over the ground.
Do not build a COLREG judgement from one AIS number in isolation.
lessons.call: When COG and heading differ, do not call one of them “wrong”. First understand what each value represents and cross-check the developing situation.

lessons.title: CPA & TCPA — prediction, not permission
lessons.body: CPA predicts the closest passing distance if the present motion continues. TCPA predicts when that closest point will occur. They are useful warning and monitoring values, but they change when either vessel manoeuvres and should not be treated as permission to stand on.
pts: Watch whether the situation is improving or deteriorating.
Collision avoidance remains a COLREG decision using all available means.
lessons.call: A small CPA deserves attention; a “comfortable” AIS CPA is not a licence to stop looking outside or stop checking radar.

lessons.title: Class A, Class B and the incomplete picture
lessons.body: AIS equipment does not all transmit identical information or at identical reporting behaviour. Small craft may use Class B, some vessels are not required to carry AIS, and some contacts may not appear at all.
pts: Common on SOLAS commercial shipping and carries the fuller shipborne data set.
Common on smaller/non-SOLAS craft; capabilities and reporting differ from Class A.
A real vessel can exist without appearing as an AIS target.
Objects and vessels may be detectable by other means even when absent from AIS.
lessons.call: The empty space between AIS symbols is not necessarily empty sea. Keep the lookout and use all appropriate sensors.

lessons.title: Stale, lost, wrong and virtual targets
lessons.body: An AIS symbol can become stale when reports stop. Incorrect sensor or manually entered data can be transmitted. AIS can also represent physical, synthetic or virtual aids to navigation, so an electronic symbol is not always a physical object at that exact position.
pts: The last report gets older; the vessel has not necessarily disappeared.
Bad input or sensor data can create misleading information.
AIS position comes from the transmitting target’s electronic position source.
Some AIS navigation marks can exist electronically without a physical buoy there.
lessons.call: If AIS and the outside/radar picture disagree, investigate the disagreement. Never force reality to fit the electronic display.

lessons.title: The safe AIS watch
lessons.body: The safest way to use AIS is as one layer in a wider watchkeeping picture. Identify, correlate, monitor trends and then apply the COLREGs using sight, hearing, radar where fitted and every other appropriate means.
pts: Maintain a proper visual and auditory lookout.
Correlate AIS with radar and the real-world picture where available.
Use all available means appropriate to determine risk of collision.
Do not let an AIS name tempt you into negotiating away clear COLREG responsibilities by radio.
lessons.call: Stage 8 principle: AIS improves situational awareness when it is cross-checked. Over-reliance on it can reduce situational awareness.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the COLREGs?
questions.explanation: The COLREGs provide internationally agreed navigation rules intended to prevent collisions at sea.

questions.prompt: Which Rule requires every vessel to maintain a proper look-out?
questions.explanation: Rule 5 is the look-out rule and applies to every vessel.

questions.prompt: Which group contains the core rules for look-out, safe speed, risk of collision and action to avoid collision?
questions.explanation: Rules 5, 6, 7 and 8 form the core sequence taught in this stage.

questions.prompt: Before deciding who gives way, what should you identify first?
options: The actual situation and applicable Rules
Which vessel has the newest electronics
questions.explanation: Helmlore teaches you to identify the navigational situation and applicable Rules before deciding obligations.

questions.prompt: What is the basic duty of a give-way vessel?
options: Maintain course and speed whatever happens
Take early and substantial action to keep well clear
questions.explanation: A give-way vessel should take early and substantial action to keep well clear.

questions.prompt: Does being the stand-on vessel mean you can stop monitoring the other vessel?
options: No — continue to monitor and be ready to act as Rule 17 requires
Yes — the other vessel has all responsibility
questions.explanation: Stand-on status does not remove the duty to keep a proper look-out and monitor the developing situation.

questions.prompt: Which Rule deals specifically with narrow channels?
questions.explanation: Rule 9 contains the narrow-channel provisions.

questions.prompt: Which Rule deals specifically with traffic separation schemes?
questions.explanation: Rule 10 deals with traffic separation schemes.

questions.prompt: Which Rule becomes central when vessels are not in sight of one another in restricted visibility?
questions.explanation: Rule 19 addresses conduct of vessels in restricted visibility when they are not in sight of one another.

questions.prompt: Is a slogan such as “power gives way to sail” enough to decide every encounter?
options: Yes — it overrides all other Rules
No — identify the applicable Rules and circumstances
questions.explanation: Simple slogans are not a substitute for identifying the vessel types, situation, environment and applicable COLREG Rules.

courses.title: Safety Awareness at Sea
courses.description: Six visual lessons on preparing, spotting hazards, protecting the crew and responding when plans change.

lessons.title: Before leaving the berth
lessons.alt: Five connected pre-departure decisions: conditions, vessel, people, equipment and fallback.
lessons.sceneAlt: Two recreational boaters wearing lifejackets review a chart and conditions before departure.
lessons.sceneCaption: Before leaving: agree the route, limits and fallback while the boat is safely alongside.
lessons.lead: A safe trip starts with a decision to go, delay, change the plan or stay alongside.
points: Conditions and limits
Check the latest forecast, tides, visibility and the crew’s ability. Decide on a clear turn-back point.
Vessel and crew
Check fuel, engine, bilges, batteries, navigation and communications. Brief every person on hazards, emergency gear and who can take over.
Tell someone
Share destination, route, crew, expected return and what to do if overdue with a reliable shore contact.
lessons.scenario: The forecast worsens and one crew member has never used the VHF. Pause departure, revise the plan and brief the crew before deciding whether to go.

lessons.title: Spot and control risk
lessons.alt: Risk assessment loop: spot hazard, identify who may be harmed, control it, brief the crew and review.
lessons.sceneAlt: Two boaters pause when they notice a loose line crossing the side deck.
lessons.sceneCaption: Look first: the loose line crosses the walking route. Secure it before anyone uses the deck.
lessons.lead: Look for what could cause harm, then change the task so the hazard is less likely to hurt anyone.
points: Spot the hazard
Examples include a wet deck, loose mooring line, anchor windlass, hot exhaust or exposed rail. Ask who might be harmed and how.
Control the source
Change or stop the task, isolate equipment, establish a safe working area and use suitable protection. A checklist alone does not remove danger.
Review as conditions change
A safe deck in harbour can become unsafe in darkness or rough water. Brief the crew and revisit controls after a change or near miss.
lessons.scenario: A mooring line now runs across the route to the foredeck. Re-route people and secure the line before the next task.

lessons.title: Stay aboard and work safely
lessons.alt: Five deck work reminders: handholds, clear route, line of pull, moving gear and rail.
lessons.sceneAlt: Lifejacket-wearing boater holds a grab rail while moving along the side deck underway.
lessons.sceneCaption: Move deliberately with a secure handhold and a clear route. Plan deck tasks before anyone leaves the cockpit.
lessons.lead: The best man overboard response is to prevent someone entering the water.
points: Control movement
Keep decks clear, move with handholds, use non-slip footwear and avoid working alone on an exposed deck where possible.
Keep clear of loaded lines

Never stand in a bight. Brief the crew on the actual line lead, possible snap-back and moving gear; the rest of the deck is not automatically safe. Stop the operation and release the load safely before dealing with a snag.
Wear suitable flotation
Choose a lifejacket appropriate to the boat, conditions and wearer. Check its fit, condition and fastenings, and follow the maker’s instructions.
lessons.scenario: While berthing a pleasure boat, a mooring line snags and comes tight. Stop hauling, keep bystanders clear and reassess how to release it without putting anyone in a bight or possible snap-back area.

lessons.title: Know and check the safety kit
lessons.alt: Original visual checklist for lifejacket, communication, fire and recovery equipment.
lessons.sceneAlt: Crew check a lifejacket and locate a throw line, VHF and extinguisher in a pleasure boat cockpit.
lessons.sceneCaption: Check fit, access and crew familiarity with the equipment aboard your own boat.
lessons.lead: Equipment helps only if it is accessible, serviceable and the crew know how to use it.
points: Personal flotation
Confirm correct fit, fastenings, service status and that each person knows how to put it on. Follow the maker’s instructions for inspection.
Alarm and communication
Know the fixed and handheld VHF, position source and emergency contacts. Keep a charged backup and explain how to raise an alarm.
Fire, flooding and recovery
Locate extinguishers, pump controls, seacocks, throw line and recovery aid. Check access and assign roles before departure.
lessons.scenario: The throw line is buried in a locker beneath luggage. Move it to an accessible position and make sure the crew can find it.

lessons.title: People and changing conditions
lessons.alt: A decision tree for fatigue, weather and an unsafe task: slow down, change plan or stop.
lessons.sceneAlt: Two recreational boaters discuss a chart and weather in a wheelhouse while safely in harbour.
lessons.sceneCaption: Changing conditions are a prompt to pause, share information and revise the plan.
lessons.lead: Fatigue, cold, pressure and distraction can turn a routine operation into a mistake.
points: Recognise fatigue
Look for slower reactions, missed checks, poor judgement or a change in mood. Arrange rest and a competent handover.
Use a stop point
Anyone should be able to say that an operation is unsafe. Pause, reassess and change the plan without blame.
Keep a margin
Reduce workload when visibility or sea state worsens. Turn back or seek shelter before options narrow.
lessons.scenario: The only person keeping lookout is struggling to stay alert. Hand over to a competent rested person or make a safe plan to stop.

lessons.title: Act early in an emergency
lessons.alt: Five response steps: alert, protect, call, manage and review.
lessons.sceneAlt: Lifejacket-wearing crew practise a man overboard drill with a training dummy in sheltered water.
lessons.sceneCaption: Practice drill: one person keeps sight and raises the alarm while the helm maintains control.
lessons.lead: A simple, rehearsed response is easier to follow under pressure.
points: Alert and protect
Raise the alarm, account for everyone and keep rescuers safe. Take immediate action only within your capability.
Call for help
Use the appropriate maritime distress or urgency procedure and give identity, position, nature of problem and assistance needed. VHF operation needs separate training.
Manage and review
Stabilise the vessel if safe, follow the emergency plan, preserve a lookout and reassess. Practise procedures with the actual crew and equipment.
lessons.scenario: A crew member falls overboard. Shout, maintain sight, alert the skipper and start the practised recovery plan while summoning help as needed.

questions.prompt: The forecast has worsened beyond your crew’s comfortable limits. What is the safer decision?
options: Delay or change the passage and reassess
Rely on the plotter to avoid the weather
questions.explanation: Departure is a decision point. Change the plan before losing easy options.
questions.alt: Fog obscuring vessels at a harbour

questions.prompt: What should a shore contact know before a passage?
options: Only the name of the boat
Route, people aboard, expected return and overdue action
questions.explanation: A useful passage plan gives a shore contact enough information to raise an appropriate alarm.

questions.prompt: A loose line creates a trip hazard on deck. What is the best first control?
options: Put up a warning and carry on
Remove or secure the line and keep the route clear
Ask the crew to step over it
questions.explanation: Control the hazard at its source rather than relying on people to avoid it.

questions.prompt: When should a task risk assessment be revisited?
options: Only when the vessel is sold
When conditions, equipment or the operation change
questions.explanation: Controls need review whenever the situation changes materially.

questions.prompt: While mooring a pleasure boat, a line snags and comes under heavy tension. What should the skipper do before anyone tries to free it?
options: Ask someone to stand outside the straight line of pull; that part of the deck must be safe
Stop hauling, keep others clear and assess the line lead, bights and possible snap-back before safely easing the load
Have a crew member step into the bight to lift the line free
questions.explanation: The danger is not limited to the straight line of pull. A snagged line can release suddenly, and the possible snap-back area depends on its lead. Stop and reassess before handling it.

questions.prompt: A line has jammed in moving machinery. What should happen first?
options: Reach in before it gets worse
Stop and isolate the machinery before handling it
Increase speed to clear the jam
questions.explanation: Remove the energy source before anyone approaches the jam.

questions.prompt: What makes a lifejacket ready for use?
options: It fits the wearer, is serviceable and is worn correctly
It is the same colour as the boat
questions.explanation: Availability alone does not make flotation effective.
questions.alt: A lifejacket checked during a boat inspection

questions.prompt: A recovery line is buried beneath equipment. What is the problem?
options: No problem if someone knows it is there
It may be inaccessible when seconds matter
It should always be kept below deck
questions.explanation: Emergency equipment should be accessible and its location understood.
questions.alt: Accessible lifebuoy secured to a ship rail

questions.prompt: A watchkeeper is making repeated mistakes from fatigue. What is the best response?
options: Arrange a competent handover or stop safely
questions.explanation: Fatigue reduces attention and judgement; change the watch arrangement.

questions.prompt: A crew member says a deck task feels unsafe. What should the skipper do?
options: Pause and reassess with the crew
Ignore it unless an accident occurs
questions.explanation: A stop point lets the crew control a developing risk.

questions.prompt: A person falls overboard. What immediate actions fit the plan?
options: Keep visual contact, raise the alarm and start recovery
Leave the helm unattended to search lockers
Wait to see if they swim back
questions.explanation: An immediate alert and maintained visual contact support recovery.

questions.prompt: When calling for help, what information is most useful?
options: Identity, position, problem and assistance needed
The price of the safety equipment
questions.explanation: Clear details help responders locate and assist the vessel.

courses.title: Tides, Heights & Streams
courses.description: Eight visual lessons and practical workshops for tidal depth, stream and passage timing.

lessons.title: The tide cycle
lessons.subtitle: Why the water rises and falls
lessons.lead: The Moon is the strongest driver of the tide; the Sun also matters. Local coastlines change the pattern you actually see.

points.title: Gravity and location
points.text: The Moon and Sun produce tidal forces. The rotation of Earth and the shape of seas and estuaries turn that forcing into local high and low waters. Many UK ports have roughly two highs and two lows a day, but timings and shapes vary.

points.title: Springs and neaps
points.text: Spring tides occur around new and full Moon when solar and lunar effects reinforce; neaps occur around quarter Moon when they partly offset. “Spring” describes the range, not the season.

points.title: Local patterns
points.text: Some ports have a stand, double high water or asymmetric rise and fall. Never assume that every location follows a smooth six-hour rise and six-hour fall.

lessons.scenario: A weekend cruise is at neaps. Does that mean the sea is necessarily calm? No. Tidal range is smaller; wind and sea state still need their own forecast.
lessons.takeaway: Check the local port prediction and the weather separately.

lessons.title: Find the prediction
lessons.subtitle: High and low water tables
lessons.lead: Start with the right place, date, time standard and source before using any number.

points.title: Read the entries
points.text: A table gives predicted times and heights of high and low water for a named port and date. The height is above the chart datum used by the product, not the water depth at your berth.

points.title: Check time and locality
points.text: Check whether the source displays UTC, local time or BST. A secondary port may require time and height corrections from a standard port; use the official product instructions.

points.title: Prediction is not observation
points.text: Atmospheric pressure, wind and other conditions can push actual water above or below a prediction. Check recent observations and local notices when clearance is tight.

lessons.scenario: A tide table says high water 14:20. Your watch and chartplotter show different zones. Resolve the time standard before planning arrival.
lessons.takeaway: Write the source, date, port and time zone in the passage note.

lessons.title: Depth under the boat
lessons.subtitle: Chart datum and clearance
lessons.alt: Depth under the boat teaching diagram
lessons.lead: Combine the charted depth with the predicted height, then allow for the boat and uncertainty.

points.title: Soundings and drying heights
points.text: A charted sounding is normally depth below chart datum. Approximate depth at a time = charted depth + height of tide. A drying height is above chart datum: approximate depth over it = height of tide − drying height.

points.title: Under-keel clearance
points.text: Approximate clearance = available depth − vessel draught. Keep an additional margin for squat, waves, heel, survey accuracy, silt and uncertainty in actual tide.

points.title: Know the reference
points.text: Do not add a tidal height to a bridge clearance or an arbitrary marina depth. Vertical clearances may use another reference level; read the chart notes and local information.

lessons.scenario: Charted depth 2.0 m, predicted height 1.5 m, draught 1.2 m: estimated still-water clearance is 2.3 m before safety allowance.
lessons.takeaway: Try the depth workshop below using training numbers.

lessons.title: Between high and low
lessons.subtitle: Tidal curves and local corrections
lessons.alt: Between high and low teaching diagram
lessons.lead: A curve shows how quickly the height changes; the middle of the tide may rise or fall fastest.

points.title: Use the curve
points.text: For an intermediate time, use the official port curve or prediction if available. Plot the correct day’s high and low waters and read the height at the required time.

points.title: Rule of twelfths
points.text: The 1–2–3–3–2–1 sketch divides a six-hour range into approximate hourly changes. It assumes a simple tide and is unreliable at ports with unusual curves, stands or double highs.

points.title: Clearance decisions
points.text: When depth matters, use current official data for the exact area, check uncertainty and leave a margin. The sketch is for understanding the shape, not a substitute for a prediction.

lessons.scenario: A shallow entrance is usable only near high water. Read its local curve and the harbour guidance instead of guessing halfway height.
lessons.takeaway: Treat every drawn curve here as schematic, never a real port prediction.

lessons.title: The water moves sideways
lessons.subtitle: Flood, ebb, set and rate
lessons.alt: The water moves sideways teaching diagram
lessons.lead: Height and stream describe different things. A tide can be high while the stream is still moving.

points.title: Language
points.text: A flood stream generally accompanies the rising phase; ebb accompanies falling. “Set” is the direction the water flows towards. “Rate” is its speed in knots.

points.title: Slack water
points.text: Slack is a period of weak or changing stream. It need not coincide exactly with high or low water, especially in channels and constricted water.

points.title: Local effects
points.text: Headlands, narrows, shallow banks and estuaries can accelerate or turn the stream. Wind against a strong stream can make steep, uncomfortable or dangerous seas.

lessons.scenario: You plan to round a headland at high water. Can you assume slack? No: consult the local stream prediction or atlas.
lessons.takeaway: Read both the height and the stream for the route.

lessons.title: Read stream information
lessons.subtitle: Atlases and tidal diamonds
lessons.lead: Match the correct hour to the reference port, then use the arrow and rate for your position.

points.title: Atlas hour
points.text: An atlas commonly shows hourly stream arrows before and after high water at a named reference port. Check which port, which high water and the publication’s time convention.

points.title: Spring and neap rates
points.text: Tidal diamonds and atlas tables may give mean spring and mean neap rates. The actual rate varies through the cycle and with location and weather.

points.title: Update the chart
points.text: Use a current authorised chart or service, correct edition and local warnings. The diagram here teaches the reading process and contains no real navigation data.

lessons.scenario: Your atlas plate is labelled HW Dover −2. Find the relevant Dover high-water time, then apply that hour to the correct place on your route.
lessons.takeaway: The reference port need not be the nearest harbour.

lessons.title: Allow for the stream
lessons.subtitle: Set, drift and course to steer
lessons.alt: Allow for the stream teaching diagram
lessons.lead: The boat’s motion through the water and the water’s motion over the ground add as vectors.

points.title: Track over ground
points.text: A boat travelling north at 4 kn through the water with a 1 kn eastward stream will, in one hour, move about 4 NM north and 1 NM east if its heading stays north.

points.title: Counter the stream
points.text: To hold a north ground track in that simplified steady example, steer about 14° west of north at 4 kn through the water. Northward progress then falls to about 3.9 kn.

points.title: Recheck underway
points.text: Log, compass, GPS track and speed over ground answer different questions. Recheck set and rate as they change; do not treat a calculated course as a guarantee.

lessons.scenario: A GPS track drifts to starboard of the intended line. First identify actual set and rate, then adjust heading and monitor the new track.
lessons.takeaway: Practice the simple drift model below; it is a teaching model.

lessons.title: Plan the tidal window
lessons.subtitle: Timing a recreational passage
lessons.alt: Plan the tidal window teaching diagram
lessons.lead: Put height, stream and weather on one timeline and build a fallback.

points.title: Depth window
points.text: Identify the least depth on the route, boat draught and a sensible margin. Work back from the predicted height at the actual transit time, including secondary-port corrections where required.

points.title: Stream window
points.text: Estimate favorable and adverse streams for each leg. A strong adverse stream changes speed over ground and arrival time; near headlands, wind against tide can matter more than an average rate.

points.title: Decision points
points.text: Check weather, daylight, harbour instructions and a safe alternative. Use current official predictions and warnings just before departure, then monitor actual conditions underway.

lessons.scenario: An entrance has enough predicted depth at 16:00 but the last leg faces a strong adverse stream. Recalculate ETA and preserve an alternative port.
lessons.takeaway: A passage plan needs both arrival time and a usable depth window.

questions.prompt: What does the height in a tide table normally measure?
options: Height above the product’s chart datum
questions.explanation: Use the named product datum and local chart.

questions.prompt: When do spring tides generally occur?
questions.explanation: The term describes a larger tidal range.

questions.prompt: A sounding is 2.0 m and the predicted tidal height is 1.5 m. What is approximate still-water depth?
questions.explanation: Add sounding and height when the references match.

questions.prompt: A drying height is 1.0 m and tidal height is 1.6 m. What is the approximate water depth over it?
questions.explanation: Subtract drying height from tidal height.

questions.prompt: Can you assume slack stream exactly at high water?
questions.explanation: Height and stream timing can differ.

questions.prompt: What does “set” describe?
questions.explanation: Rate is speed; set is direction.

questions.prompt: Which high water is relevant to a stream atlas labelled HW at a reference port?
options: The named reference port’s high water
Any high water on the same day
questions.explanation: Match the reference port and hour in the publication.

questions.prompt: A 1 kn eastward stream acts on a northbound boat for one hour. About how far east does water carry it?
questions.explanation: Distance = speed × time in this simplified constant-stream example.

questions.prompt: What is the best basis for a constrained shallow-water transit?
options: Current local prediction, chart, corrections and safety margin
A tide height from any nearby port
questions.explanation: Allow for local and weather-related uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Why check wind against tide?
options: It can produce steep, rough seas
It always raises the predicted high water
questions.explanation: Waves can steepen against a strong current.

questions.prompt: What should you check before using a published tidal time?
questions.explanation: UTC/BST and locality errors affect the whole plan.

questions.prompt: What does a negative result in a depth margin calculation mean?
options: The chosen allowance is not met in the model
questions.explanation: Replan with current local data and an adequate margin.

courses.title: Boat Systems & Stability
courses.description: Eight visual lessons on loading, watertight integrity, propulsion, fuel, electrical power and steering.
courses.alt: AI-generated photographic scene of a recreational motorboat in a marina

lessons.title: How a boat stays upright
lessons.subtitle: Buoyancy and righting
lessons.lead: A boat floats when it displaces enough water to support its weight. Its ability to recover from heel also depends on hull shape, loading and openings.
points: Buoyancy
The hull displaces water and supports the boat. More load generally increases displacement and draught; it does not automatically improve safety.
Heel and recovery
A sideways force heels the boat. Hull form, ballast and the centre of gravity affect how it responds. A quick snap upright is not proof of a safe stability margin.
Boat-specific limits
Use the builder’s manual, capacity and loading information for the actual vessel. A training sketch cannot establish safe heel angles or loading limits.
lessons.scenario: A crew member says a heavily loaded boat feels solid because it rolls less. Is that enough evidence? No. Check the loading limits, freeboard and how the weight is distributed.
lessons.takeaway: A comfortable motion is not a stability certificate.

lessons.title: Load low, secure and within limits
lessons.subtitle: People, gear and tanks
lessons.lead: Where weight sits matters as much as how much is aboard.
points: High weight
Heavy items on a roof or flybridge raise the centre of gravity. Keep stores low where the builder permits and secure them against movement.
Side-to-side balance
Do not gather everyone on one side or use a permanent list as a reason to add arbitrary counterweight. Find the cause.
Liquid movement
Water in a partly filled space can shift as the boat heels. Free water in a bilge or on deck is especially concerning; remove it and find the source.
lessons.scenario: Several heavy boxes are stacked on the cabin roof for a trip. Move them to approved low stowage, secure them and check total loading.
lessons.takeaway: Check weight, position, restraint and the boat’s limits.

lessons.title: Keep the water outside
lessons.subtitle: Openings, drains and bilges
lessons.lead: Stability can deteriorate quickly if water enters or stays aboard.
points: Openings
Know the location and purpose of seacocks, through-hulls, hatches and doors. Keep closures accessible and use them as specified for the conditions.
Drains and pumps
Check cockpit drains, bilge pump modes, alarms and manual means of removing water. A pump manages water; it does not repair an ingress source.
Investigate early
Unexpected bilge water, a new list or repeated pump cycling requires prompt action: protect people, locate and control ingress if safe, and seek help early.
lessons.scenario: The automatic bilge pump cycles repeatedly. Do not treat the pump as the fix. Find the inflow, prepare a safe return or call for assistance.
lessons.takeaway: Keep openings sound, drainage clear and water ingress visible.

lessons.title: Propulsion and cooling
lessons.subtitle: Engine, raw water and exhaust
lessons.lead: Understand the flow of energy and cooling well enough to spot a problem before propulsion is lost.
points: Before starting
Check fuel, oil, coolant when cold, belts where accessible, leaks and the raw-water intake or strainer as the vessel manual directs.
While running
Watch the instruments, alarms and exhaust water where applicable. A temperature alarm, lost cooling flow or new smell needs prompt response.
Safe response
Reduce load or stop the engine as appropriate, assess the situation, avoid hot pressurised coolant and rotating machinery, and follow the engine manual.
lessons.scenario: The temperature alarm sounds and exhaust water flow has stopped. Reduce load, move to a safe situation, stop as directed and investigate without opening a hot coolant cap.
lessons.takeaway: Know your normal readings and respond to change.

lessons.title: Fuel and range
lessons.subtitle: Supply, filtration and reserve
lessons.lead: A reliable fuel supply means more than a gauge showing fuel in the tank.
points: Follow the path
Identify the tank, shutoff, filters or water separator, engine feed and return where fitted. Know which valves are normally open.
Contamination
Water or debris can block filters and stop an engine. Inspect and maintain to the manufacturer’s schedule; protect filler and vent fittings.
Reserve
Plan range using realistic consumption and a margin for weather, delay and diversion. Never rely on the last indicated litres.
lessons.scenario: An engine loses power in rough water and a fuel filter alarm appears. Prioritise sea room and crew safety, then follow the boat’s fault procedure; do not randomly switch valves.
lessons.takeaway: Know the system and carry a realistic fuel reserve.

lessons.title: Electrical power aboard
lessons.subtitle: Batteries, charging and isolation
lessons.lead: Know what supplies the essential circuits and how to isolate a fault.
points: Sources and loads
Identify start and domestic batteries, alternator, shore power, charger, inverter and labelled distribution panels where fitted.
Protection
Fuses and breakers protect wiring. Repeated trips, heat, smell or damaged cable require investigation, not a larger fuse or repeated resets.
Isolation
Know the master switches and shore-power disconnect. Use approved procedures for your system; high-current DC and mains equipment need competent work.
lessons.scenario: A navigation-light breaker trips again after one reset. Use the appropriate alternative lighting and make a safe plan; do not fit a higher-rated breaker.
lessons.takeaway: Preserve essential power and investigate abnormal heat or trips.

lessons.title: Steering and control
lessons.subtitle: Helm, drive and backups
lessons.lead: Steering relies on several linked parts; know what you can check and what backup the boat actually has.
points: Normal path
Helm input may reach rudder, outboard or drive mechanically, hydraulically or electronically. Locate the relevant controls and indications.
Pre-departure
Check helm response, gear engagement and steering space in safe conditions. Watch for leaks, unusual resistance or unexpected autopilot behaviour.
Loss of control
Reduce speed, warn the crew, establish sea room, use a documented backup only if fitted and appropriate, and call for help before options run out.
lessons.scenario: The wheel turns but the boat does not respond. Disengage autopilot if relevant, reduce speed, assess the steering system and seek assistance early.
lessons.takeaway: A backup must be known and checked, not assumed.

lessons.title: A practical fault routine
lessons.subtitle: From warning to safe decision
lessons.lead: A good skipper notices the first abnormal sign, protects the crew and chooses a safe course before a minor fault becomes urgent.
points: Notice
Brief the crew on normal sounds, smells, gauges, bilge level and alarms. Record what changed and when.
Stabilise
Keep clear of hazards, reduce demand on the failing system, use suitable safety equipment and communicate the situation.
Decide
Use the boat-specific manual and competence available. If propulsion, steering, flooding or fire threatens safety, seek help early using the appropriate distress or urgency procedure.
lessons.scenario: A persistent bilge alarm and loss of charging occur together. Treat them as related until checked: protect crew, inspect for ingress if safe, conserve power and call for help as needed.
lessons.takeaway: People and sea room first; diagnose only when safe.

questions.prompt: The boat feels steadier after heavy equipment is added to the roof. Does that show its stability is adequate?
options: Yes, less rolling proves the loading is safe
No. Comfortable motion does not establish adequate stability
Yes, roof-mounted equipment always lowers the centre of gravity
questions.explanation: How a boat feels is not a stability assessment. High-mounted weight can raise the centre of gravity and reduce stability. Check the loading arrangement and the vessel’s limits rather than judging safety from the motion alone.

questions.prompt: What is the best place for heavy stores?
options: Low, secure and in approved stowage
questions.explanation: Use the builder’s loading guidance and secure stores.

questions.prompt: What is free water in a bilge likely to do?
options: Move as the boat heels and worsen stability
questions.explanation: Shifting free water is a serious concern.

questions.prompt: An automatic bilge pump runs repeatedly. What next?
options: Find the source and make a safe plan
questions.explanation: A pump does not fix ingress.

questions.prompt: When is it safe to open a hot pressurised coolant cap?
options: Only as directed after the system has cooled
questions.explanation: Hot coolant can cause serious burns.

questions.prompt: A cooling alarm sounds and exhaust water flow stops. What first?
options: Respond promptly and follow the boat’s procedure
Wait for the alarm to clear
questions.explanation: Reduce load or stop the engine as the vessel’s procedure directs, when safe to do so. Investigate loss of cooling water before restarting; continuing to run can cause serious damage.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a fuel plan?
options: A realistic reserve for delay and diversion
questions.explanation: Allow a sensible reserve.

questions.prompt: A breaker trips repeatedly. What should you do?
options: Replace it with a larger rating
Investigate the fault and use safe alternatives
questions.explanation: The protective device indicates a fault.

questions.prompt: What should you know about the battery system?
options: Sources, essential loads and isolation points
questions.explanation: Know how essential power is supplied and isolated.

questions.prompt: The boat stops answering the helm. What is sensible?
options: Reduce speed, gain sea room where possible and assess backups
questions.explanation: Reduce the immediate risk, use available sea room and follow the boat’s emergency-steering procedure. Seek help early if control cannot be restored safely.

questions.prompt: What should you check about emergency steering on your own boat?
options: Assume the normal helm has an automatic backup
Whether it is fitted, and how the manufacturer says to use it
Assume every boat can be steered by disconnecting the steering cable
questions.explanation: Emergency steering arrangements vary. Find out whether your boat has one, where its equipment is kept and how to use it, following the vessel’s instructions.

questions.prompt: A new list and bilge alarm occur together. What priority?
options: Protect crew and investigate ingress if safe
Add weight on the opposite side
questions.explanation: Treat potential flooding promptly.

courses.title: Understanding Compass
courses.description: Start with four visual steps on the compass circle, heading, bearings and ground track. Then explore eight detailed lessons.
courses.alt: AI-generated photographic close-up of a marine steering compass

lessons.title: Read the compass circle
lessons.subtitle: Cardinal and halfway points
lessons.lead: Nautical directions are written as three-digit degrees measured clockwise from north. A full turn brings you back to north.
points: Four main points
North 000° (also 360°), east 090°, south 180°, west 270°.
Halfway points
Northeast 045°, southeast 135°, southwest 225°, northwest 315°. These are convenient anchors, not the only directions.
At the helm
The fixed lubber line is aligned with the bow. Read the card where it meets that line, allowing for boat motion and compass settling.
lessons.scenario: The card shows 075° C at the lubber line. The bow points between northeast and east; it is not a bearing to an object.
lessons.takeaway: Name a direction in three digits and say which reference it uses.

lessons.title: Heading, bearing and planned course
lessons.subtitle: Three different questions
lessons.lead: First decide what the number describes: bow direction, direction to an object, or the course you intend to make.
points: Heading
The direction the bow points at that moment. Read it from a suitable heading instrument.
Bearing
The direction from the observer to a charted or identified object. A handheld bearing compass is useful for sighting it.
Planned course
The direction of a planned leg on the chart, with its reference stated. Steering adjustments may be required to achieve the intended track.
lessons.scenario: A lighthouse bears 045° C while the bow points 090° C. Both can be true: the lighthouse lies to port of the bow.
lessons.takeaway: Ask “direction of what, from where, and relative to which north?”

lessons.title: Heading is not your track
lessons.subtitle: Through water and over ground
lessons.lead: A moving boat has several directions. Current and leeway can separate the bow, movement through the water and movement over the ground.
points: Heading
Where the bow points. It does not by itself tell you where the boat is moving.
Through-water course
The direction of movement relative to the surrounding water, affected by leeway. It is not established by the compass heading alone.
Course over ground
The direction of movement across the Earth while moving, commonly shown as GNSS COG. At very low speed it can be unstable.
lessons.scenario: A boat points 090° C while COG reads 105°. Check the actual track and position; this difference alone cannot calculate the current.
lessons.takeaway: Use independent position checks to see whether you are following the plan.

lessons.title: Two practical compass tools
lessons.subtitle: Steering and hand bearing
lessons.lead: The fixed compass helps hold a heading. A handheld bearing compass lets you sight an object. Each reading has a job.
points: Steering compass
Fixed in the boat, with a lubber line pointing forward. Its reading is the compass heading.
Hand bearing compass
Portable and aimed at a visible object to read its compass bearing. Identify the object before using it for navigation.
Check the surroundings
Nearby metal, magnets and powered equipment can disturb magnetic instruments. Use the actual compass correctly and know its limitations.
lessons.scenario: You want a lighthouse bearing while steering. Use an appropriate handheld bearing compass, sight the identified lighthouse and record the time and C reference.
lessons.takeaway: A heading instrument and a sighting instrument answer different questions.

lessons.title: True and magnetic north
lessons.subtitle: Variation depends on place and time
lessons.lead: Charts use true north. Earth’s magnetic field provides magnetic north, and the angular difference is called variation.
points: True north
The geographic chart reference. Mark a true direction with T.
Magnetic north
The Earth-field reference. Mark a magnetic direction with M; a boat compass may also have its own error.
Find local variation
Use current chart or authoritative variation information for the position and date. No single UK number is valid everywhere or forever.
lessons.scenario: You plan 080° T on a chart. The same 080 number on a magnetic compass does not automatically make the same direction.
lessons.takeaway: Check the local variation before comparing chart and magnetic directions.

lessons.title: Deviation belongs to the boat
lessons.subtitle: Heading-specific compass error
lessons.lead: Metal and equipment aboard can make the steering compass differ from the local magnetic reference. This is deviation.
points: Boat influence
Ferrous metal, magnets and electrical equipment near the compass can affect it.
Not one fixed value
Deviation can vary with the vessel’s heading. Use current, applicable boat-specific deviation information.
Check and correct
A suspect compass needs competent assessment. Keep portable magnetic objects away and do not improvise adjusters.
lessons.scenario: A speaker has been installed beside the compass. Do not assume the old deviation information remains valid.
lessons.takeaway: Variation belongs to the place; deviation belongs to the boat.

lessons.title: Convert between compass and chart
lessons.subtitle: C → M → T
lessons.lead: Do the two corrections separately, writing C, M and T after each result. Sample values here are fictional.
points: Boat correction
082° C with 2° E deviation gives 084° M: add east, subtract west when moving from C to M.
Place correction
084° M with 4° W variation gives 080° T: add east, subtract west when moving from M to T.
Reverse carefully
To work from T back to C, undo variation then deviation. Check that the deviation applies to the intended heading and wrap around 000–359°.
lessons.scenario: Do not put 082° C directly on a true chart in this example. Correct it through M to obtain 080° T.
lessons.takeaway: C + signed deviation = M; M + signed variation = T.

lessons.title: Plot and verify a bearing
lessons.subtitle: From object to chart line
lessons.lead: A measured compass bearing can provide a line of position after applying the appropriate corrections and confirming the object.
points: Measure and label
Sight an identified charted object, note time and record the reading as C (or the instrument’s actual reference).
Convert and plot
Convert to true before plotting on a true chart. The line from the object back toward you uses the reciprocal direction, 180° opposite the bearing to the object.
Do not overclaim
One bearing gives a line of position, not a complete fix. Cross-check with a second bearing, a transit or other independent observation as appropriate.
lessons.scenario: A lighthouse bears 045° T from the boat. The boat lies somewhere on the reciprocal 225° T line from the lighthouse; one line alone does not fix the boat’s position.
lessons.takeaway: Identify, measure, correct, plot and cross-check.

questions.prompt: What is the compass direction of east?
questions.explanation: East is 090° clockwise from north.

questions.prompt: What is northeast?
questions.explanation: Northeast is halfway from north to east.

questions.prompt: Where do you read a steering compass heading?
questions.explanation: The lubber line points forward with the boat.

questions.prompt: What is the heading?
questions.explanation: Heading describes bow direction.

questions.prompt: What is a bearing?
options: Direction from observer to an object
questions.explanation: A bearing points towards the object from the observer.

questions.prompt: A lighthouse bears 045° while the bow heads 090°. What does this mean?
options: The lighthouse is in a different direction from the bow
questions.explanation: The object can lie off the bow.

questions.prompt: What is a handheld bearing compass mainly used for?
options: Sighting the direction to an object
questions.explanation: It is a sighting instrument.

questions.prompt: What does GNSS COG normally show while moving?
questions.explanation: COG describes the ground track.

questions.prompt: Can heading and COG alone reveal exact current?
questions.explanation: Leeway and other factors also matter.

questions.prompt: Which north is a nautical chart direction referenced to?
questions.explanation: Chart directions use true north.

questions.prompt: What is variation?
questions.explanation: Variation is associated with Earth’s field, place and date.

questions.prompt: What is deviation?
questions.explanation: Deviation is the boat compass error relative to magnetic.

questions.prompt: 082° C plus 2° E deviation gives what?
questions.explanation: Add east moving C to M.

questions.prompt: 084° M with 4° W variation gives what true direction?
questions.explanation: Subtract west moving M to T.

questions.prompt: A lighthouse bears 045° T from you. Which line from it can your boat lie on?
questions.explanation: The reciprocal 225° T line runs back from the object to the observer.

questions.prompt: Does one bearing to a charted lighthouse give a complete fix?
options: No; it gives a line of position
questions.explanation: A second independent line or observation is needed for a fix.
