courses.title: Chart Work & Position
courses.description: Read realistic training charts, plot positions, take visual fixes, build DR and EP, and cross-check GPS.
courses.alt: AI-generated photographic scene of a chart table with dividers and parallel ruler

lessons.title: Read the chart before plotting
lessons.subtitle: Scale, depths, symbols and reliability
lessons.lead: Choose a chart with enough detail for the job. First read its title, scale, units, datum, edition, corrections and notes.
points: Scale matters
A larger-scale chart such as 1:10,000 shows a smaller area in more detail than 1:100,000. Enlarging a small-scale image does not add survey detail.
Read the water

Soundings are charted depths; contours join equal depths. Rocks, wrecks and drying areas need careful interpretation using the chart legend and an appropriate symbol reference. Colour alone is not a safe-depth test.
Check its limits
Position datum and vertical chart datum are different. Check source information, survey quality, notes and updates. Our original chart has invented depths and geography and is only for training.
lessons.scenario: On Alder Bank the charted depth is 4.6 m. A fictional tide height of 1.8 m gives 6.4 m water depth. With 1.6 m draught, static clearance is 4.8 m before allowances for waves, squat, uncertainty and a chosen safety margin.
lessons.takeaway: A chart is evidence with limits. Use current, suitable-scale chart information for navigation.

lessons.title: Read and plot latitude and longitude
lessons.subtitle: Degrees, minutes and hemispheres
lessons.lead: Read latitude first, then longitude. Check both the number format and N/S/E/W.
points: Read the sides
Latitude increases northwards on this chart. P lies on 50°04.000′ N. One degree contains 60 minutes, and a minute can be divided into decimal fractions.
Read the top or bottom
Longitude is 004°10.000′ W. West minutes get smaller as you move east. Extend the longitude line vertically and the latitude line horizontally on a north-up Mercator chart.
Formats are different
50°04.000′ N equals 50.066667° N and 50°04′00″ N. Decimal degrees are not degrees and decimal minutes. A west longitude is negative when written as signed decimal degrees.
lessons.scenario: A GPS shows 50.066667, −4.166667 in decimal degrees. Convert to approximately 50°04.000′ N, 004°10.000′ W before using the border scales.
lessons.takeaway: Keep the format, datum and hemispheres with the coordinates.

lessons.title: Measure distance and time
lessons.subtitle: Dividers and the latitude scale
lessons.lead: On a Mercator chart, take the distance with dividers and transfer it to the latitude scale close to the measured line.
points: Distance
One minute of latitude is approximately one nautical mile. Longitude minutes are narrower at this latitude and are not a nautical-mile distance scale.
Speed and time
Distance in NM = speed in knots × time in hours. Thirty minutes is 0.5 hours. Time in minutes = distance ÷ speed × 60.
Use the right speed
Speed through water belongs in a through-water dead-reckoning calculation. Speed over ground belongs in a ground-distance calculation. Tide can change the arrival time.
lessons.scenario: P to Q is 3.0 NM. At a constant ground speed of 6 kn, the leg takes 30 minutes. At 4 kn over ground, it takes 45 minutes.
lessons.takeaway: Say whether your speed and distance are through water or over ground.

lessons.title: Plot a course on the chart
lessons.subtitle: True direction and chart tools
lessons.lead: A plotted line gives a direction over the chart. It does not automatically give the compass heading to steer.
points: Draw the leg
Identify the start and destination accurately, draw the intended track and inspect the whole corridor for hazards. A direct line may be unsafe.
Measure from true north
Use a plotter or parallel rules to measure clockwise from true north. P to Q is 090° T, due east. Label the direction and distance.
Convert in separate steps

Allow for stream and leeway when shaping the course, then convert true to magnetic to compass using current variation and the boat’s applicable deviation. The compass pathway teaches those corrections.
lessons.scenario: A chart leg measures 090° T. Before steering, ask what current will do, whether leeway matters, and which compass corrections apply. Do not simply steer 090° C.
lessons.takeaway: Planned track, through-water course and compass heading are different quantities.

lessons.title: Fix your position with two bearings
lessons.subtitle: Observe, convert, plot, cross-check
lessons.lead: A bearing to an identified charted object gives a line on which your boat lies. A second suitable bearing gives a crossing.
points: Observe and identify
Choose clearly identified fixed landmarks with a useful angle between them. Take the bearings close together in time and record time and instrument reference. Avoid nearly parallel lines.
Plot the lines
Convert compass observations to true bearings as necessary. From each landmark draw the reciprocal direction back towards the observer. A bearing of 000° T to A gives a southward line from A.
Interpret the crossing
A bears 000° T and B bears 090° T in this ideal example. Their lines meet at P. Real bearing error, vessel movement and wrong identification can make the result unreliable.
lessons.scenario: Plot from Alder Light south on 180° T, and from East Light west on 270° T. The two lines meet at 50°04.000′ N, 004°10.000′ W.
lessons.takeaway: The bearing is from your boat to the object; the plot from the object uses the reciprocal.

lessons.title: Use a third line and judge the uncertainty
lessons.subtitle: Fix quality, cocked hats and other observations
lessons.lead: A third independent observation checks the first two. Real position lines rarely meet perfectly.
points: Third bearing
A third identified landmark provides another line. Our chart shows an idealised common intersection; actual observations may form a small triangle called a cocked hat.
Do not trust the centre blindly
A triangle is not a guarantee that the boat is inside it. Wrong identification or systematic error can put every line in the wrong place. Check the observations and allow clearance from danger.
Other methods

A transit gives a position line through two objects seen in line. A radar range gives a distance circle around an identified fixed target. A bearing and range can form a fix. An echo-sounder depth is a check, not normally a unique position.
lessons.scenario: Your plotted fix is near a shoal but the coast looks wrong. Reduce exposure to danger, check landmark identity, bearing reference and time, and take another independent observation.
lessons.takeaway: The quality of the observations matters more than the neatness of the crossing.

lessons.title: Dead reckoning: advance the last fix
lessons.subtitle: Direction and distance through the water
lessons.lead: Dead reckoning, or DR, calculates a new position from a known starting position, course and distance through the water, before adding current.
points: Start with a timed fix
P is the 10:00 fix. Convert steering information to a usable true reference. For this first example, leeway is zero and the through-water course is 090° T.
Calculate the run
6 kn × 30/60 h = 3.0 NM. Plot 3.0 NM east from P and mark it DR 10:30. In a real log, plot at changes of course or speed as well as at suitable intervals.
Remember what is missing
DR is a calculated position, not a new observation. Steering errors, speed errors and unmodelled movement accumulate. Obtain another fix rather than allowing the uncertainty to grow unchecked.
lessons.scenario: DR 10:30 is approximately 50°04.000′ N, 004°05.326′ W. It has not yet been moved by the current.
lessons.takeaway: DR answers where the boat would be from the through-water run alone.

lessons.title: Estimated position: add the stream
lessons.subtitle: Set, rate and leeway
lessons.lead: Estimated position, or EP, includes estimated environmental movement. Add vectors over the same elapsed time.
points: Name the stream correctly
Set is the direction towards which the current flows. A stream setting 000° T flows north. At 2 kn for 30 minutes, it carries the boat 1.0 NM.
Move the DR
From DR 10:30 draw 1.0 NM north, using the same 30-minute period. Mark the result EP 10:30. Do not use a full hour of tide for a half-hour run.
Add other effects carefully
Include a justified leeway allowance in the through-water direction when relevant. Avoid double-counting it. Streams and wind vary; an EP remains an estimate, so seek a fresh observed fix.
lessons.scenario: In this short-leg exercise, EP 10:30 is approximately 50°05.000′ N, 004°05.326′ W. The 1.0 NM northward displacement is the modelled stream, not a measurement of actual current.
lessons.takeaway: Fix + through-water movement + estimated environmental movement = EP.

lessons.title: Shape a course to counter the stream
lessons.subtitle: An introduction to the course-to-steer triangle
lessons.lead: To keep an intended eastward ground track when the stream sets north, the boat must move partly south through the water.
points: Work in one reference
For this exercise the desired track is 090° T, speed through water is 6 kn, and the stream is 2 kn towards 000° T. Assume constant stream and no leeway.
Balance the sideways movement
The southward component of the boat’s movement must cancel 2 kn north. The true course to steer is about 109.5° T, and resulting ground speed is about 5.66 kn east.
Finish the practical job

Convert true course to magnetic and compass separately. Check the chart corridor, wind, tide changes and your observed track. A calculated course is a starting estimate, not an instruction to ignore what you see.
lessons.scenario: Over 30 minutes the boat moves about 2.83 NM east and 1.0 NM south through water. The stream adds 1.0 NM north, leaving about 2.83 NM east over ground.
lessons.takeaway: Aim into the sideways current and verify the ground track.

lessons.title: Use GPS without surrendering the navigation
lessons.subtitle: Position, datum, COG, SOG and independent checks
lessons.lead: GPS is one satellite constellation within GNSS. A receiver supplies a position; the chart and navigator give that position meaning.
points: Transfer it correctly
Check the fix status, timestamp, coordinate format and chart datum. Modern charts commonly use WGS 84, but verify yours. Extra decimal places do not prove equal accuracy.
Read the right direction
COG is movement over the ground; SOG is speed over the ground. COG is not bow heading and may become unreliable at very low speed. A heading sensor is a separate input.
Cross-check independently

Compare with identified visual objects, radar where fitted and suitable, and depth with tide accounted for. Two displays sharing one receiver are not independent. Power loss, stale data, interference, jamming or spoofing can mislead you.
lessons.scenario: The GPS dot shows open water but a correctly identified transit and depth disagree. Treat the discrepancy as a navigation problem immediately; do not follow the dot into possible danger.
lessons.takeaway: A convincing screen does not remove the need for a lookout and independent position checks.

lessons.title: Bring chart work into harbour pilotage
lessons.subtitle: Depth, marks and a simple entry plan
lessons.lead: As you approach the coast, switch from broad passage navigation to detailed pilotage. Use the largest suitable chart and local information.
points: Plan the entry
Write a short sequence of recognisable features, directions, distances and depth checks. Include local rules, weather, tide, traffic, an abort point and somewhere safe to wait.
Understand the marks

Our training harbour uses IALA Region A: entering from seaward, red port-hand marks lie to port and green starboard-hand marks to starboard. Check the local direction of buoyage; lateral marks are not a complete pilotage plan.
Keep the crew involved
Brief the lookout, helm and navigator. Keep a safe speed, monitor depth and confirm each feature. Do not let chart work pull attention away from collision avoidance or the water ahead.
lessons.scenario: Identify both entry lights before committing to the harbour. If the expected marks or depths do not match, stay clear of danger and reassess rather than pressing on.
lessons.takeaway: A safe entry uses the chart, the conditions and what the crew actually observes.

lessons.title: Record, check and navigate when a screen fails
lessons.subtitle: A practical navigation routine
lessons.lead: Keep a clear record so the next position can be checked and the plan can survive a lost screen or uncertain fix.
points: Record enough to reconstruct it
Write position, time, source of fix, course reference, speed basis and significant changes. Label fix, DR and EP distinctly. Use a consistent time reference and record any change.
Match the checking interval to risk
Fix more often near hazards, at higher speed, in restricted visibility, or when information disagrees. There is no universal safe interval for every boat and location.
Have an independent alternative

Plan how to confirm position and reach safety if the primary equipment fails. It may be paper chart work, independent electronics or other suitable methods; make sure the alternative really works without the failed source or power supply.
lessons.scenario: Your chartplotter loses power. Use the last timed fix and log to start DR/EP, seek visual or other independent observations, maintain a lookout and act conservatively while position confidence is reduced.
lessons.takeaway: Keep the basic navigation working before relying on extra features.

questions.prompt: Which chart offers more detail for a harbour entry?
options: 1:10,000, if current and suitable for the area
Either chart gains new detail when enlarged
questions.explanation: A larger-scale chart has a smaller scale denominator and normally shows more local detail.

questions.prompt: Where do you measure distance on this Mercator chart?
options: The latitude scale near the measured line
questions.explanation: One minute of latitude is approximately one nautical mile.

questions.prompt: How long is 3 NM at a constant 6 kn over ground?
questions.explanation: Time = 3 ÷ 6 hours = 0.5 hours.

questions.prompt: The charted depth is 4.6 m and tide height is 1.8 m. What is water depth in the example?
questions.explanation: Add height above chart datum to charted depth, before clearance and uncertainty allowances.

questions.prompt: A point is at 004°10′ W. Moving east makes its west minutes…
options: smaller, until reaching zero at Greenwich
questions.explanation: Eastward movement approaches zero west longitude.

questions.prompt: 50.066667° N is approximately…
questions.explanation: Multiply the fractional degree by 60 to obtain minutes.

questions.prompt: A lighthouse bears 045° T from the boat. Which reciprocal direction runs from the lighthouse back towards the boat?
questions.explanation: Add 180° and wrap within a full circle.

questions.prompt: Which pair of position lines normally gives a better-defined crossing?
options: One bearing taken twice without accounting for movement
Two well-separated, correctly identified bearings taken close together in time
questions.explanation: A useful crossing angle improves geometry, but observation accuracy and timing still matter.

questions.prompt: Is the boat guaranteed to be inside a three-bearing cocked hat?
options: No; systematic errors or misidentification can put it outside
Only if the triangle is drawn neatly
questions.explanation: Investigate the observations and allow for uncertainty, especially near danger.

questions.prompt: A transit is…
options: two identified objects seen in line, providing a position line
a line joining two different tide times
questions.explanation: An identified transit is useful independent positional evidence.

questions.prompt: For a through-water DR run, which speed is appropriate?
options: GPS SOG without checking the distinction
questions.explanation: Match the speed basis to the run being plotted.

questions.prompt: 6 kn through water for 30 minutes gives…
questions.explanation: Thirty minutes equals 0.5 hours.

questions.prompt: A current setting 000° T flows…
questions.explanation: Set is the direction towards which the current moves.

questions.prompt: A 2 kn stream over 30 minutes displaces the boat by…
questions.explanation: Use the same elapsed time as the vessel run: 2 × 0.5 = 1 NM.

questions.prompt: How does EP differ from the basic DR example?
options: It is always an observed fix
It removes the need to take another fix
questions.explanation: Adding stream and relevant leeway does not make the result an observation.

questions.prompt: To make an eastward track against a north-setting stream, you need a through-water direction with…
questions.explanation: The southward component counters the stream; calculate the amount and verify the result.

questions.prompt: At very low boat speed, GPS COG…
options: may be unstable and is not a substitute for heading
questions.explanation: COG describes movement over ground, not the direction the bow points.

questions.prompt: Which is an independent check of a GPS position?
options: Another screen sharing the same receiver
The precision of its decimal places
A visual fix from correctly identified landmarks
questions.explanation: A separate observation source can reveal a shared electronic error.

questions.prompt: What should you do when the GPS position disagrees with reliable visual evidence?
options: Investigate immediately and keep clear of danger
Follow the GPS because electronics cannot be wrong
Ignore the view and enlarge the screen
questions.explanation: Treat contradictions as a navigation problem and use other available evidence.

questions.prompt: In our Region A harbour, entering from seaward, the port-hand mark is…
options: red, on the vessel’s port side
a direction to pass every red object to starboard
questions.explanation: Check the direction of buoyage and local information.

questions.prompt: How often should a navigator obtain fixes?
options: Often enough for speed, hazards, visibility and confidence in the information
questions.explanation: The interval must suit the risk rather than an arbitrary fixed rule.

courses.title: Passage Planning & Logbook
courses.description: Build a sensible passage plan, prepare alternatives, monitor the journey and keep a useful navigation log.
courses.alt: AI-generated photographic scene of a skipper planning a passage

lessons.title: Start with a trip you can safely make
lessons.lead: A passage plan is your answer to: where are we going, can we do it safely, and what will we do if things change?
points: Match the trip to the boat
Check seaworthiness, range, draught, equipment and the kind of conditions the boat can handle.
Match the trip to the crew
Consider experience, fatigue, seasickness and whether someone else can take over. A shorter sheltered trip may be the better choice.
Keep the plan proportionate
Even a short outing needs planning. A longer or exposed trip needs more detail. Planning is a continuing process, not a form to complete once.
lessons.example: A two-hour coastal outing with a novice crew may be unsuitable if the return is exposed to worsening wind. Change the destination or postpone.
lessons.remember: Choose a suitable trip before choosing a departure time.

lessons.title: Gather the information before drawing a route
lessons.lead: Use current information, check its date, and write down the assumptions that could change.
points: Read the right sources
Use suitable current charts, harbour information, pilot books, notices and navigation warnings. Inspect an electronic route at a useful detailed scale.
Check weather and sea state
Look at wind direction and strength, gusts, waves, visibility and the trend for the return journey. Wind against tide can make conditions worse.
Check local constraints
Confirm access, berth availability, tidal gates, lock or bridge operation and local rules. Identify the forecast and tide time zones: UTC and BST differ by one hour.
lessons.example: An arrival at 14:00 BST is 13:00 UTC. A gate time copied without its time basis can leave you an hour late.
lessons.remember: Current information and a clear time basis underpin the plan.

lessons.title: Plan the whole route, berth to berth
lessons.lead: A route includes leaving the harbour, the open-water legs and the final approach.
points: Keep clear of hazards
Choose waypoints with a considered safety margin from shoals, rocks and other dangers. A waypoint is a reference point, not proof that the line to it is safe.
Inspect every leg
Check the complete corridor between waypoints, including traffic, prohibited areas and potential drift. Auto-routing suggestions need independent inspection.
Prepare the pilotage
Write the arrival sequence before you leave: marks, transits, channel directions, speed restrictions and a place to wait or turn around.
lessons.example: The fictional blue route bends around East Island. The dashed direct line crosses the island: a straight line to the destination is not a navigable route.
lessons.remember: Check the water between the waypoints, not just the waypoint positions.

lessons.title: Use tides to choose an arrival window
lessons.lead: Height tells you about depth; stream tells you about movement. Both can constrain your timing.
points: Calculate available depth
Where depth and tide height use the same chart datum, available depth = charted depth + tide height. Subtract draught to find static clearance.
Allow for uncertainty
Account for waves, squat where relevant, survey quality, loading and tide prediction uncertainty. Choose a suitable margin for this boat and location.
Work backwards from a gate
Identify when depth or access is sufficient, allow for travel and waiting, and review the plan if delayed. Do not rush an unsafe approach to catch a gate.
lessons.example: Fictional sill: 0.8 m charted depth + 2.0 m tide = 2.8 m water. With 1.6 m draught, static clearance is 1.2 m before other allowances. These are invented teaching figures.
lessons.remember: A tidal gate is a constraint to respect, not a deadline to chase.

lessons.title: Estimate leg times and a realistic ETA
lessons.lead: Use expected speed over ground for travel time. Through-water speed alone does not include the stream.
points: Calculate each leg
Time in hours = distance in nautical miles ÷ expected speed over ground in knots. Allow separately for harbour manoeuvres and waiting.
Make the uncertainty visible
Plan a reasonable range of arrival times. Slower progress can affect tide, fuel, daylight and the conditions at the destination.
Recalculate underway
Compare observed progress with the estimate. An ETA is a forecast to update, not an appointment the boat must keep.
lessons.example: Teaching legs of 6 NM and 4 NM at 5 kn take 72 and 48 minutes. Add 30 minutes for manoeuvres and waiting: 2 h 30 min. Depart 09:00, estimate arrival 11:30, using one stated time basis.
lessons.remember: Distance ÷ speed over ground gives time; delays need their own allowance.

lessons.title: Plan endurance and keep a reserve
lessons.lead: Know how long the boat can operate, and preserve options if the trip becomes longer.
points: Use evidence from your boat
Estimate fuel burn at the planned operating conditions from reliable measurements or appropriate manufacturer data. Include auxiliary use and other consumers.
Include the alternative
Allow for manoeuvring, delays, a diversion and a reserve appropriate to the circumstances. There is no single reserve percentage suitable for every voyage.
Verify usable fuel
Check levels, usable capacity, tank selection and fuel condition. For sailing boats also consider the possible need to motor. Check water, food, power and crew endurance.
lessons.example: At an assumed 8 L/h, 2.5 h uses 20 L. A one-hour diversion adds 8 L and a chosen illustrative reserve adds 10 L: 38 L total. The 10 L is an example, not a universal rule.
lessons.remember: Plan for the trip changing, not only for the shortest route.

lessons.title: Choose alternatives and decision points
lessons.lead: Decide what would make you delay, turn back or divert while there is still room to do it.
points: Name a usable alternative
A nearby harbour is not automatically a refuge. Check its approach, depth, shelter for the forecast direction and whether entry will be possible.
Set triggers in advance
Examples include worsening visibility, crew illness, an equipment fault or missing a safe entry window. Define limits suitable for this boat, crew and passage.
Keep a way out
Identify where you can wait, return or divert before committing to a restricted approach. Review the consequences of an engine or navigation failure.
lessons.example: If the arrival window is missed, the plan calls for a checked waiting area or a suitable alternative. Entering with insufficient clearance is not an acceptable shortcut.
lessons.remember: Prepare the alternative before you need it.

lessons.title: Brief the crew and tell someone ashore
lessons.lead: Make the plan understandable to the people who may need to help you.
points: Explain the journey
Cover destination, timing, likely conditions, roles and when you might change the plan. Show the crew the arrival sketch and safety equipment.
Prepare for the skipper being unavailable
Someone should know how to stop or control the boat, call for help and give its position. Confirm the available communication equipment.
Leave a shore plan
Tell a responsible person the boat, people aboard, route, expected return or arrival and what to do if concerned. Update them when plans change and close the plan on arrival.
lessons.example: If you divert, tell the shore contact when it is safe to do so. An unchanged expected-return message can cause avoidable concern.
lessons.remember: A shared plan works better than a plan only the skipper understands.

lessons.title: Keep a log that helps you navigate
lessons.lead: The passage plan records your intentions. The navigation log records observations, decisions and what actually happened.
points: Record a useful snapshot
Include date and time basis, position and source, heading or course with reference, COG/SOG where useful, weather, depth with reference and relevant machinery or fuel observations.
Distinguish evidence from estimates
Label a visual fix, GPS fix, DR or EP clearly. Record changes of course, incidents, reasons for decisions and the revised ETA.
Keep entries timely and safe
Use an interval suited to speed, hazards and workload. Record significant events. Maintain lookout and control first; do not become absorbed in typing.
lessons.example: 10:00 UTC — GPS fix cross-checked by transit; SOG 4 kn instead of planned 5 kn; crew seasick. Decision: reduce exposure, review diversion and update ETA. A position alone would not explain the decision.
lessons.remember: Record enough to reconstruct your navigation and explain your decisions.

lessons.title: Monitor, change the plan and close the passage
lessons.lead: Keep asking whether the original assumptions still hold, then finish with a useful record.
points: Compare plan with reality
Monitor position independently, progress, depths, weather, traffic, fuel and crew condition. A route drawn earlier does not guarantee safe water now.
Act on differences
If circumstances change, evaluate the remaining route and alternatives. Record the decision, brief the crew and update the shore contact when appropriate.
Close and learn
Record arrival, secure the boat, tell the shore contact and note defects or lessons. Keep a backup of the log and improve the next plan.
lessons.example: A delay and worsening sea state invalidate the intended arrival. The skipper selects a checked alternative, updates the crew and shore contact, and records the reason.
lessons.remember: A good plan changes when the evidence changes.

questions.prompt: What should determine the detail of a passage plan?
options: The boat, crew, route and risks
questions.explanation: Keep planning proportionate to the proposed trip.

questions.prompt: Does a short local outing need planning?
questions.explanation: Short trips can still involve weather, hazards and access constraints.

questions.prompt: What must you inspect after an automatic route is suggested?
options: Every leg and its surrounding hazards at a suitable chart scale
questions.explanation: Automation does not establish that the proposed corridor is safe.

questions.prompt: What speed is used for estimated travel time?
options: Speed through water without considering current
questions.explanation: Travel time depends on progress over the ground.

questions.prompt: How long is 6 NM at 5 kn over ground?
questions.explanation: 6 ÷ 5 hours equals 1.2 hours or 72 minutes.

questions.prompt: Why must a tide prediction’s time basis be checked?
options: UTC and local summer time can differ
A clock setting never affects planning
questions.explanation: Identify time zone, date and daylight-saving status.

questions.prompt: Depth 0.8 m plus tide 2.0 m, with draught 1.6 m, gives what static clearance?
questions.explanation: 0.8 + 2.0 − 1.6 = 1.2 m. Check matching datums and uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What makes a harbour a suitable alternative?
options: Checked access and shelter for the expected conditions
Being the nearest name on the chart
questions.explanation: Depth, conditions, approach and availability matter.

questions.prompt: What do you do if a safe tidal-entry window is missed?
options: Enter anyway to keep the ETA
questions.explanation: Do not chase a gate at the expense of safety.

questions.prompt: What should a fuel estimate include?
options: Expected use, delays or diversion and a suitable reserve
A universal percentage for every boat
questions.explanation: Use realistic boat-specific information and preserve alternatives.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a plan and a log?
options: The plan states intentions; the log records reality
The log is only for engine hours
questions.explanation: Use the log to compare actual progress and decisions with intentions.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a logged position?
questions.explanation: The source distinguishes an observation from DR or EP.

questions.prompt: How often should you log observations?
options: As appropriate to hazards, speed and workload, and at significant events
Exactly once an hour on every voyage
questions.explanation: Choose an interval that supports safe monitoring.

questions.prompt: What should happen after a diversion?
options: Replan, brief the crew and update the shore contact when safe
questions.explanation: Record the reason and communicate the change.

questions.prompt: What takes priority over entering a log on a screen?
options: Lookout and safe control of the boat
questions.explanation: A log supports navigation and must not distract from it.

courses.title: Diesel Engine Basics
courses.description: Learn the engine cycle, checks, filters, diesel bug, cooling, servicing and sensible fault finding through visual lessons.

lessons.title: Meet your engine
lessons.lead: A small marine diesel needs clean fuel, air, lubrication, cooling and enough electrical power to start.
points: Start with its identity
Find the engine model, serial number and gearbox model. Obtain the correct manuals: engines that look similar can have different pumps, filters and service procedures.
Locate the owner’s checks
Use your manual to find the dipstick, oil filler, fuel filters, coolant check point, raw-water strainer and pump, belt, battery isolation and stop control.
Learn the boundaries
The lessons explain a typical four-stroke inboard diesel. Mechanical injection is our fuel-path example; common-rail engines have different controls and high-pressure precautions.
lessons.example: A four-cylinder Volvo Penta and a four-cylinder Beta share basic principles. Their component locations, fluids and service instructions are not interchangeable.
lessons.remember: Know what each component does before trying to service it.

lessons.title: How a four-stroke diesel works
lessons.lead: Air goes in, gets hot under compression, fuel burns, and exhaust goes out. Four piston strokes make one complete cycle.
points: Intake and compression
The intake valve opens as the piston moves down and draws in air. Both valves then close; the rising piston compresses and heats that air.
Power and exhaust
Fuel is injected near the end of compression and ignites in the hot air. Expanding gas pushes the piston down. The exhaust valve opens for the upward exhaust stroke.
Starting is different from running
The starter turns the engine initially. A diesel uses compression ignition, not a petrol-style spark plug. Glow plugs or other starting aids are model-dependent; follow their instructions.
lessons.example: The cycle takes two crankshaft revolutions. Four cylinders repeat it at different times to produce more even power.
lessons.remember: Air + compression + correctly delivered fuel = combustion.

lessons.title: Before starting: a calm check
lessons.lead: Check with the engine stopped and cool, then keep hands and clothing clear when it runs.
points: Fluids and supply
Check engine oil, coolant and gearbox oil using the specified methods. Confirm usable fuel, the required fuel valve position, and an open cooling seacock for normal starting afloat.
Look, smell and inspect

Look for fresh fuel, oil or coolant leaks; check the bilge, hoses, clamps and belt condition. Inspect the raw-water strainer safely. Close its seacock before opening where flooding is possible, reseal and reopen before running.
Prepare the boat and crew

Ventilate, secure the boat, confirm neutral, ensure the propeller area is clear and keep people away from rotating parts. Follow the manual’s start procedure. Check cooling discharge and instruments after starting; a dry exhaust or continuing alarm needs prompt action.
lessons.example: A loose strainer lid can draw air even with the seacock open. After reassembly, check for a good seal, leaks and restored cooling flow.
lessons.remember: Oil, coolant, fuel, seawater supply and a clear engine space.

lessons.title: Follow the fuel from tank to cylinder
lessons.lead: There is a low-pressure supply side and a high-pressure injection side. They do different jobs.
points: Supply and clean
In our mechanical-injection example, fuel passes from tank and shutoff valve through a primary filter/water separator, lift pump and engine-mounted fine filter.
Meter and inject
The injection pump delivers timed high-pressure fuel through rigid lines to injectors in the cylinder head. Modern common-rail systems use a rail and electronically controlled injectors.
Return and protect

Surplus fuel returns to the tank in this example. Actual routing varies. Never search for a pressure leak with your hand, loosen high-pressure lines to bleed, or dismantle injectors as a beginner. Injection injuries require urgent medical attention.
lessons.example: If the engine loses power after rough water, disturbed tank contamination may restrict the filters. That is a possibility to investigate, not a diagnosis.
lessons.remember: Clean the fuel before it reaches the expensive injection equipment.

lessons.title: Filters, water and air in the fuel
lessons.lead: A separator removes water and particles; a fine filter protects the injection system. Air in the supply can stop the engine.
points: Inspect the separator

Water collects low in a suitable separator. Follow its maker’s method for inspection and draining into a container with the engine stopped. Some units have a metal bowl or sensor rather than a clear bowl.
Change the right element

Use the specified element and filtration rating. Contain spills, keep connections clean, check old seals have been removed, fit the correct new seals and follow the tightening instructions. Do not pour unfiltered fuel into a clean outlet.
Prime only as instructed

Filter changes or an empty tank may introduce air. Some engines self-prime; others use a hand pump and specified low-pressure bleed points. Follow the exact manual. Recheck for leakage and dependable running before departure.
lessons.example: An engine starts briefly after a filter change, then stops. First consider incomplete priming or an air leak at the new seal; do not start undoing injector pipes.
lessons.remember: Water and air do not belong in the fuel supply.

lessons.title: Diesel bug: recognise and prevent it
lessons.lead: Microbes can grow where water and diesel meet. Their debris can block filters, but dark sludge alone does not prove diesel bug.
points: Recognise the clues

Recurring blocked filters, slime and water contamination justify investigation. Dirt, corrosion products, aged fuel and wax can also cause restrictions. A fuel sample or specialist testing helps distinguish the cause.
Remove the conditions

Buy fuel from a reliable source, inspect filler seals and vents, keep water out, check the separator and manage fuel age. Tank inspection and removal of accumulated water may require a competent specialist.
Treat the whole problem

A suitable approved biocide may be part of a confirmed treatment plan, with correct compatibility and dosage. Killing microbes does not remove sludge or dead biomass; tank cleaning, fuel treatment and filter replacement may still be needed.
lessons.example: A new filter blocks again soon after treatment. Debris may still be reaching it. Repeatedly adding more chemical is not a substitute for investigating and cleaning the contaminated system.
lessons.remember: Prevent water ingress; investigate repeated contamination.

lessons.title: Cooling: two separate water circuits
lessons.lead: On a heat-exchanger-cooled engine, engine coolant and seawater exchange heat while staying separate.
points: Closed coolant circuit

A circulation pump moves the specified coolant through the engine. A thermostat controls temperature and flow to the heat exchanger; a bypass may circulate coolant during warm-up. Check level only by the manual’s safe cool-engine method.
Open raw-water circuit

Seawater enters through the hull seacock and strainer, passes through the raw-water pump and heat exchanger, then commonly joins the wet exhaust. Gearbox coolers and anti-siphon arrangements may also be fitted; their order is installation-specific.
Watch for lost cooling

A shut seacock, blocked strainer, air leak, damaged impeller or fouled exchanger can reduce cooling. No normal discharge, steam or a rising temperature needs prompt attention. Never remove a hot pressurised coolant cap. Running ashore requires an approved raw-water supply; do not run this cooling system dry.
lessons.example: The exhaust suddenly sounds hollow and dry. Treat that as a possible raw-water supply failure; do not wait for the temperature alarm before responding.
lessons.remember: Coolant cools the engine; seawater carries the heat away.

lessons.title: Raw-water pump and impeller
lessons.lead: A flexible rubber impeller moves raw water. Its position and drive depend on the engine: belt-driven and gear-driven arrangements both exist.
points: Understand the part

Flexible vanes change shape in the pump housing to move water. It is not the engine’s coolant circulation pump. A photograph of a belt-driven Yanmar pump is one real example, not the layout of every four-cylinder engine.
Recognise damage
Cracked, set, worn or missing vanes can reduce flow. Dry running can damage an impeller rapidly. A failed shaft seal can leak; pump replacement or seal work may need an engineer.
Check the complete circuit

Stop the engine, prevent accidental starting and close the cooling seacock before opening a pump that could admit water. Use the manual for service. Recover missing vane pieces from downstream components; a new impeller does not clear an obstructed heat exchanger.
lessons.example: The old impeller has one vane missing. Replacing it is only part of the job: the missing piece may have travelled into a cooler or heat exchanger.
lessons.remember: A missing vane is also a possible blockage downstream.

lessons.title: Oil, lubrication and the gearbox
lessons.lead: Oil carries load between moving surfaces, reduces wear and helps manage heat. The engine and gearbox have separate requirements.
points: Read the level correctly

Use the manual’s dipstick procedure, boat attitude and waiting time. Keep within the specified marks; too little and too much oil can both cause problems. Gearbox level methods may differ, including whether its dipstick is screwed in.
Use the correct products
Oil grade, specification, quantity and filter depend on engine and gearbox. A gearbox may require a different fluid entirely. Service at the stated hours or calendar interval, whichever is due first.
Understand an oil-and-filter service

The visual sequence is: identify the correct oil and filter, stop and make safe, contain and remove old oil, replace the filter and seal as specified, refill to the correct level, then perform the manual’s leak/level checks. Warm oil may drain more easily but can burn; never work beside moving machinery.
Recognise warning signs

Unexpectedly rising oil level, milky oil, fuel smell or metal debris requires investigation. A low-oil-pressure warning while running is urgent; adding oil does not automatically cure low pressure. Do not keep running to see if it clears.
lessons.example: The oil level has risen above maximum without topping up. That may indicate contamination. Stop treating the dipstick as reassurance and have the cause checked.
lessons.remember: Oil level and oil pressure are different things.

lessons.title: Starting battery, alternator and belts
lessons.lead: The battery supplies cranking power. Once running, the alternator normally recharges it through the boat’s charging system.
points: No crank or slow crank

Check the approved starting sequence, neutral interlock where fitted, correct battery bank and isolator position. A discharged battery, loose or corroded connection, cable fault or starter fault are possible causes. Do not bridge terminals. Observe the manual’s cranking limits and pauses. Repeated cranking of a wet-exhaust engine can accumulate seawater and cause hydraulic lock; use its model-specific procedure, not a universal seacock rule.
Inspect with the engine stopped

Look for cracked, glazed or frayed belts and loose connections. Belt tension and routing are model-specific; keep fingers, clothing and tools away when running. A belt may drive cooling equipment as well as the alternator.
Respond to charging faults

A continuing charge warning may indicate belt, alternator or wiring trouble. A mechanically injected engine may keep running, but an electronic engine can depend on electrical power. Do not disconnect the battery or operate its isolator while the engine runs unless the manufacturer explicitly permits it.
lessons.example: The charge light stays on and the belt is damaged. Before assuming you can continue on battery power, find out what else that belt drives.
lessons.remember: Cranking, charging and cooling may be connected by one fault.

lessons.title: Air, exhaust and interpreting smoke
lessons.lead: An engine needs a clear air supply and a sound exhaust system. Colour is a clue, not a reliable diagnosis on its own.
points: Air and carbon monoxide

Check ventilation and the specified air cleaner with the engine stopped. Exhaust leaks can expose people to carbon monoxide, including from diesels. Maintain alarms and exhaust components; keep outlets clear and do not run in poorly ventilated enclosed spaces.
Read the whole picture

Persistent black smoke can relate to excess load or insufficient air; blue smoke can indicate oil burning; white smoke can be unburned fuel or other faults. Steam may indicate inadequate raw-water cooling. Compare temperature, load, duration and cooling flow.
Know when to stop investigating

A significant exhaust leak, serious overheating, abnormal knocking or fuel leakage needs immediate action to protect people and the boat. Maintain control, stop the engine when safe and appropriate, and seek assistance if needed.
lessons.example: A white plume with rising temperature and reduced exhaust water is different from brief cold-start smoke. The accompanying observations change the urgency.
lessons.remember: Smoke colour gives a starting point, not a verdict.

lessons.title: Service planning, spares and winter care
lessons.lead: Use the engine and gearbox manuals to build a service schedule. There is no universal marine-diesel interval.
points: Plan by hours and time

Record model, serial number, hours, date, parts and work done. Include first-service requirements, oil and filters, fuel filters, belts, impeller, coolant, hoses, heat exchanger and anodes where fitted. Obtain specialist help for adjustments and high-pressure work.
Carry useful, correct spares

Suitable fuel filters, an impeller and its cover seal, approved belts, fluids and the tools you can safely use may be valuable. Knowing the part numbers and having the manuals is as important as the box of spares.
Prepare for storage

Follow the manufacturer’s preservation procedure for expected frost and lay-up duration. Closed-loop antifreeze does not automatically protect the raw-water circuit. Do not dry-run the impeller; manage batteries and fuel, and collect fluids for proper disposal. Recommission before use.
lessons.example: An engine runs few hours this year. Calendar-based service can still be due. Its raw-water cooling circuit also needs its own winter plan.
lessons.remember: A service record turns “probably done” into something you can check.

questions.prompt: What causes ignition in a normal diesel cycle?
options: Heat from compressing air, with fuel injected at the right time
A petrol-style spark plug firing continuously
The alternator directly heating the fuel
questions.explanation: Diesel combustion uses compression ignition. Starting aids depend on the engine.

questions.prompt: How many crankshaft turns make one four-stroke cycle?
questions.explanation: Intake, compression, power and exhaust take two crankshaft revolutions.

questions.prompt: What is the best first step in learning the service points?
options: Use a picture of any green engine
Assume every four-cylinder engine is the same
Find the model and correct operator’s manual
questions.explanation: Component locations and procedures vary between models.

questions.prompt: Where does separated water normally collect in a suitable fuel separator?
options: At the bottom of its collection space
At the top of the air filter
questions.explanation: Water is denser than diesel. Follow the separator maker’s inspection and draining method.

questions.prompt: A filter change introduces air. What should you do?
options: Follow the specified low-pressure priming or self-priming procedure
questions.explanation: Do not open high-pressure injection lines as a beginner.

questions.prompt: What does dark sludge in a fuel filter prove?
options: It needs investigation; diesel bug is only one possible cause
questions.explanation: Dirt, aged fuel, wax and microbial contamination can cause restrictions.

questions.prompt: Why can filters block after biocide treatment?
options: Dead biomass and other debris can remain in the fuel system
questions.explanation: Treatment may need cleaning and debris removal as well as compatible approved biocide.

questions.prompt: In a normal heat exchanger, what happens to coolant and seawater?
options: They mix to cool the engine
They exchange heat without normally mixing
questions.explanation: The two circuits are normally separate.

questions.prompt: The raw-water exhaust discharge disappears. What is the sensible response?
options: Wait until the oil light appears
Increase rpm to force the blockage through
Maintain boat safety and respond promptly to possible cooling failure
questions.explanation: Do not wait for overheating to become severe.

questions.prompt: When is a pressurised coolant cap safe to open?
options: Only when cooled and according to the manual
With a cloth while it is still very hot
questions.explanation: Hot pressurised coolant can cause severe burns.

questions.prompt: An impeller has a missing vane. What else needs attention?
options: Locating the missing piece in downstream cooling components
questions.explanation: Debris can obstruct a cooler or heat exchanger.

questions.prompt: Is the raw-water pump always driven by the alternator belt?
options: No; pump location and drive vary by engine
questions.explanation: Belt-driven and gear-driven arrangements exist.

questions.prompt: Low oil pressure is indicated while running. What should you do?
options: Treat it as urgent, maintain safety and stop to investigate
Add extra oil above maximum and carry on
Assume that normal oil level makes it harmless
questions.explanation: Normal level does not prove adequate pressure.

questions.prompt: Can engine oil automatically be used in the gearbox?
options: Yes, all marine gearboxes use it
No; use the gearbox’s specified fluid and checking method
Only if the engine has four cylinders
questions.explanation: Some gearboxes need different fluid and procedures.

questions.prompt: What is a safe basic check for slow cranking?
options: Bridge starter terminals with a screwdriver
Check approved start settings, battery condition and connections safely
questions.explanation: A weak battery or poor connection is possible, but not the only cause.

questions.prompt: When should belt condition be checked by hand?
options: With the engine stopped and accidental starting prevented
questions.explanation: Rotating belts and pulleys can trap fingers and clothing.

questions.prompt: What does white smoke always mean?
options: No single diagnosis; consider start conditions, cooling flow and other signs
questions.explanation: Steam and smoke can have different causes. Use the whole set of observations.

questions.prompt: How should service intervals be chosen?
options: By using one interval for every brand
From the correct manual, considering running hours and calendar time
questions.explanation: First-service requirements and normal intervals also differ.

questions.prompt: Does engine coolant antifreeze automatically protect the raw-water side in winter?
options: No; the raw-water circuit needs the specified separate preservation procedure
Yes, the circuits are always mixed
Only when the alternator belt is new
questions.explanation: Normal heat-exchanger circuits remain separate.

questions.prompt: A high-pressure fuel leak is suspected. What should a beginner do?
options: Feel for the leak with a finger
Keep clear, make the boat safe, stop as appropriate and get qualified help
Undo the pipe to release pressure while running
questions.explanation: Pressurised fuel can penetrate skin. Do not open the high-pressure side.
